Macro Economics Impacting Investors
To understand how economies function and how they influence our financial decisions, we
first need a basic idea of what economics covers. 
Before diving deeper, let’s define both. Our main focus here is on macroeconomics and its
relevance to personal finance - a link that will become clearer as we progress.
Microeconomics studies the behavior of individuals, households, and
firms. It explores how income, prices, and production decisions
influence spending and consumption.
Macroeconomics, on the other hand, examines the overall performance of
an economy. it deals with large-scale factors like GDP, inflation, industrial
production, crude oil, and foreign exchange. Essentially, it helps us
understand whether the economy is performing well. A strong economy
generally leads to rising share and bond prices, while a weak one tends to
push them down.
Economics helps us understand how resources are produced, distributed, and consumed, both
at an individual and national level. It is mainly divided into two branches -
Microeconomics and Macroeconomics

Definition 
GDP stands for Gross Domestic Product. It is the total market value of all final goods and
services produced within a country during a specific time period, usually one year. In other
words, GDP shows the size and health of a country’s economy by adding up all the things
people make and do for pay.

[page 6]
Macro Economics Impacting Investors
7.2 - Key Indicators for Investors & Its Impact
What Counts in GDP?
Goods and Services: Both physical products (like food,
clothes, cars, and houses) and services (like haircuts,
health check-ups, renting a car, or cleaning services) are
included. For example, buying a new car adds its price to
GDP. Renting a car also counts as GDP because you are
paying for a service.
Current Production Only: GDP only includes goods and
services made during this year. If you sell old things, like a
used laptop, this transaction does not count toward GDP.
Only the original sale of that laptop by the manufacturer
is included.
Why is GDP Important?
Measurement: GDP gives a single number to measure how much a country produces in a
year.
Economic Growth: If GDP goes up, it usually means the economy is growing and people are
doing more business and earning more.
Stocks & Investments: A higher GDP can make stock markets and investments perform
better.
GDP Formula & It’s Impact
GDP = C + I + G + (X-M)
C - here denotes consumption, which includes services, non-durables, and durables
I – denotes the expenditure, which consists of expenditure on housing and equipment.
G - represents government expenditure, which includes salaries of employees,
construction of roads and railways, airports, schools and expenditure on the army

ousing and equipment.
G - represents government expenditure, which includes salaries of employees,
construction of roads and railways, airports, schools and expenditure on the army
( X - M ) - denotes total exports (X) minus total imports (M), is called net exports
A rise in GDP indicates a country’s economy is expanding while
falling GDP rates shows an economic contraction.

How Inflation is Measured?
Inflation
Inflation is tracked by seeing how the average
price of a basket of everyday items changes
over time. In India, the main way to measure
inflation is the Consumer Price Index (CPI).
Types of Price Indexes:
Wholesale Price Index (WPI): This tracks price changes at the wholesale (business-to-business)
level, focusing mostly on manufacturing goods. WPI matters to industries and uses over 700
different items to monitor price changes. The government reports WPI every month, using
2011-12 as the base year.
Consumer Price Index (CPI): This tracks retail prices—the ones we pay in shops—for around 200
items (including food, clothes, and services). CPI shows the price changes that impact everyday
consumers and is published monthly. The new base year for the Consumer Price Index (CPI) is
2024, officially replacing the previous 2012 base.
As a PFP, we should look at CPI.
The RBI also considers the CPI when deciding on policy, and it is tracked worldwide as well.
7
Meaning
Inflation means that the prices of goods and services—like food, clothes, transportation, and
entertainment—are going up over time. When inflation happens, each rupee buys less than
before, so your money doesn’t go as far as it used to. For example, if the price of a bottle of

ertainment—are going up over time. When inflation happens, each rupee buys less than
before, so your money doesn’t go as far as it used to. For example, if the price of a bottle of
oil goes from ₹100 to ₹180 in a year, that’s inflation in action!

[page 8]
Macro Economics Impacting Investors
7.2 - Key Indicators for Investors & Its Impact
Effects Of Inflation
A small amount of inflation is actually good. It
encourages people to produce more and
expand businesses, which creates jobs and
supports economic growth. But if prices go
up too quickly, it can hurt businesses and
consumers—making it hard for everyone to
manage their budgets.
For example, if a business owner expands and raises the price of cookies from ₹20 to ₹25,
there’s inflation—but also benefits like more jobs and growth in the community. Still, if the price
gets too high, people may stop buying.
Unemployment Rate
"Number of Unemployed" means people actively searching for work.
"Labor Force" means both those who have jobs and those looking for jobs.
Why Does the Unemployment Rate Matter?
Shows Economic Health: Economists look at the unemployment
rate to see how strong or week the economy is. When businesses
are confident, they hire more people; when times are tough or
uncertain (like during a financial crisis or a pandemic), companies
mght cut jobs to survive.
Tracks Change Over Time: If today’s unemployment rate is lower than last year’s, it means
more people found jobs and fewer need government support.. If it’s higher, the reverse us true.
8
Meaning
The unemployment rate shows what percentage of a country’s workforce is actively looking

und jobs and fewer need government support.. If it’s higher, the reverse us true.
8
Meaning
The unemployment rate shows what percentage of a country’s workforce is actively looking
for a job but can’t find one. The workforce is made up of people who are currently employed
(like payroll or contract workers and the self-employed) and those who are job hunting.
People not working due to age (like kids and the elderly) aren’t included.

[page 9]
Macro Economics Impacting Investors
7.2 - Key Indicators for Investors & Its Impact
How the Unemployment Rate Affects Investment?
Stock Markets: A rising unemployment rate typically makes investors nervous because it
can signal lower corporate earnings and slower economic growth, which can lead to a
decline in stock prices.
Interest Rates: Central banks (like the RBI in India) watch the unemployment rate closely. If
unemployment is high, they might lower interest rates to encourage businesses to invest
and hire. If unemployment is very low and there’s a risk of inflation, they might raise rates
to cool the economy.
Consumer Confidence: High unemployment makes people less willing to spend money,
since they’re worried about their jobs. This can hurt businesses like retail and travel.
Real Estate: More unemployment can mean fewer people can afford houses, so home sales
and prices might drop. If more people are working, housing demand rises.
Bond Markets: When unemployment is up, investors may put more money in safe places
like government bonds, which affects bond prices and yields.

Base Year: The IIP is calculated using the base year 2011-12
(value = 100). For example, if the IIP was 140 in 2019, it
means industrial activity grew by 40% compared to 2011-12.

Manufacturing (largest share, about 75% of IIP)

Meaning
The Index of Industrial Production (IIP) helps us track how the industrial sector of India is
doing. It mainly tells us how various parts of industry—like mining, electricity, and
manufacturing—are performing. The IIP is released every month by the National Statistical
Office (NSO).

Think of the IIP as a scoreboard for India’s factories, mines, and power plants. If the score goes
up, it means these industries are producing more, which helps the economy grow. If it goes
down, it might mean the economy's facing issues, and fewer goods are being made.
Crude Oil
Understanding Rupee Depreciation and Appreciation with Oil Prices
When the rupee depreciates, it loses value compared to the dollar, so
India needs to spend more rupees for every dollar's worth of oil.
For example: If ₹75 buys $1 one year and ₹80 the next, importing oil
just got more expensive for India, and you'll need more rupees to
send the same amount of dollars abroad.
When the rupee appreciates, it gains value, making each dollar
cheaper to buy, helping India save on its huge import bill for oil.
For exports, a weaker rupee means foreign buyers need fewer
dollars to purchase the same amount of Indian goods, which can
be good for exporters but bad for import expenses like crude oil.
Why Do Oil Prices Rise and What Happens?
Import Dependency: India’s heavy reliance makes it sensitive to global supply and price
shocks.
Global Supply & Demand: Oil prices are controlled by supply and demand and by groups like
OPEC and OPEC+. If these countries cut production, prices go up; if they boost production,

Global Supply & Demand: Oil prices are controlled by supply and demand and by groups like
OPEC and OPEC+. If these countries cut production, prices go up; if they boost production,
prices fall. Bringing oil wells back online is costly, so production cuts can last a while.
Recently, oil prices have risen after pandemic-related cuts in supply and a rebound in
demand with economies reopening. More demand with limited supply pushes prices higher.
10
Meaning
Crude oil is one of the world’s most important commodities, and for India, it’s especially
crucial. India is the third-largest consumer and imports nearly 89% of its crude oil, meaning
changes in global oil prices hit the country hard and quickly. Because crude oil is priced in
dollars, whenever global oil prices rise, India has to pay more dollars to buy its oil—but if the
rupee weakens against the dollar, it takes even more rupees to cover the cost, making it a
double blow to the economy.

[page 11]
Fiscal Policy
Meaning
Fiscal Policy refers to the use of government spending & tax policies to influence economic
conditions, especially macroeconomics conditions. These include aggregate demand for goods
& services, employment, inflation, & economic growth. During a recession, the government
may lower tax rates or increase spending to encourage demand & spur economic activity.
Conversely to combat inflation, it may raise rates or cut spending to cool down the economy.

What Higher Oil Prices Mean for India
Current Account Deficit: A $1/barrel rise in oil prices can
increase India’s oil bill by about $1.6 billion a year, worsening
the country’s trade deficit.
Inflation: Higher oil prices mean costlier petrol, diesel, and
everyday goods, making living more expensive. Production
and transport become pricier, squeezing household budgets
and raising inflation.
Rupee Effects: High oil prices mean India needs more dollars,
weakening the rupee further, which makes all imports more
expensive and can hurt the value of the currency.
Rising oil prices increase travel and transport costs for both households and businesses, leading
to higher expenses and reduced spending power. As production and shipping become costlier,

il prices increase travel and transport costs for both households and businesses, leading
to higher expenses and reduced spending power. As production and shipping become costlier,
prices of goods may rise. Investors and oil-dependent industries must monitor oil trends

These two rates are powerful tools the RBI uses to control money flow in the country. Imagine
them as switches for controlling how banks handle money.

Repo Rate: When banks need money, they borrow from RBI by paying interest at this rate.
Reverse Repo Rate: When banks have extra money, they deposit it with RBI and earn interest

Meaning
Monetary policy means the methods used by a country’s central bank (in India, that’s the RBI)
to manage money supply, interest rates, and the availability of credit. The goal is to keep the
economy healthy—encouraging growth, stable prices, and efficient financial markets.

For example, if the repo rate is 4%, banks will offer you a fixed deposit rate that’s a bit higher,
like 5%. For loans such as a home loan, banks might charge 2% above the repo rate, so if repo
is 4%, your loan rate may be 6%.
The repo rate is always higher than the reverse repo rate, so banks don’t profit just by
bouncing money back and forth between borrowing and depositing with RBI

have much money to spend, though if they have
any plans of buying something like a car/house,
etc., they may postpone it.
Balance Growth & Inflation with Rate Movements
To boost the falling economy RBI will decrease the rates to increase the supply of money
in the form of loans to the people/companies. It simply means RBI lets the people
spend/consume more and helps in the growth of the economy.
To control the rising inflation, RBI will increase the rates to decrease the supply of money
in the market, then people will stop spending more and consume less or they may
postpone their plans/settle for the lesser things i.e., demand reduction. Results in lowering
the inflation.

postpone their plans/settle for the lesser things i.e., demand reduction. Results in lowering
the inflation.
15
Summary 
For a PFP, understanding how the RBI uses repo rate changes to manage economic growth and
inflation is important. When rates fall, borrowing and spending increase, supporting economic
growth; when rates rise, borrowing and spending reduce, helping control inflation.

[page 16]

How Macroeconomics Influences Investments?

How Macroeconomics Influences Investments
What Happens in a Boom?
What Happens in a Recession?
7.4 - Relationship Between Macroeconomics & Investments
7.4
Relationship Between
Macroeconomics & Investments
Macroeconomics and investing are tightly linked because changes in the overall economic
environment directly shape where—and how—people invest their money. Understanding this
connection will help you make smarter investment choices, especially when the economy goes
through booms or recessions.
Interest Rates: When central banks lower interest rates, it's cheaper to borrow money, so
people and companies are more likely to invest in things like houses or new businesses.
High rates make borrowing expensive, slowing down investments.
Key Economic Factors that Affect Investments
Inflation: This means rising prices. Some inflation can be good for growth, but high or
unpredictable inflation hurts investment returns unless you earn more than inflation eats
away.
Economic Growth: During times of growth (a "boom"), companies expand and invest.
When growth slows down (a "recession"), investment opportunities shrink.
Government Policies: Changes in taxes, spending, and trade rules can make investing
riskier or more profitable.

Government Policies: Changes in taxes, spending, and trade rules can make investing
riskier or more profitable.
Currency Exchange Rates: When investing overseas, changes in currency values can boost
or shrink your profits.
16

[page 17]
Macro Economics Impacting Investors
7.4 - Relationship Between Macroeconomics & Investments
Confidence: High consumer and business confidence boosts investing. If people are
worried, investment drops.
Market Cycles: Expansion (boom) and contraction (recession) phases create different kinds
of opportunities and risks.
A macroeconomic boom means the economy is growing faster than usual.
Here’s what to expect:
What Happens in a Boom?
Key Indicators:
GDP goes up
CPI (a measure of inflation) goes up
The unemployment rate goes down
Equities (stocks) rise, as companies earn more—investors chase big gains.
Bonds fall, as investors prefer riskier assets with higher returns.
Gold drops since people feel confident in the economy.
REITs (real estate trusts) may lose appeal as interest rates rise.
Cash becomes less attractive; people want riskier investments for higher growth.
Investment Impact:
A macroeconomic recession is when the economy shrinks—output is down, jobs are lost, and
business slows.
What Happens in a Recession?
Key Indicators:
GDP falls
CPI drops
Unemployment rate rises
17

[page 18]
Macro Economics Impacting Investors
7.4 - Relationship Between Macroeconomics & Investments
Equity investments may decline as company earnings and investor sentiment weaken.
Investors often shift towards bonds for more stable and predictable returns.
Gold generally performs well because investors prefer safer assets during uncertain times.
REITs may remain relatively stable as they continue to generate rental income and dividend
yields.
Investors usually increase their cash holdings to reduce risk and maintain liquidity.
Investment Impact:
Macroeconomic changes like booms and busts affect investment returns, risks, and decisions.
By keeping an eye on economic trends and matching your investments to the current cycle,
you’ll have a better chance at reaching your financial goals—while staying prepared for
whatever the economy has in store.
18
Summary 
For a PFP, understanding the relationship between macroeconomic conditions and investments
is essential. Factors such as interest rates, inflation, economic growth, and government policies
influence market cycles and investment performance. By recognizing how investments behave
during economic booms and recessions, PFPs can better interpret market movements and guide
clients with clearer economic context.

What is Macro Economics?
Macro economics is the branch of economics that studies how an overall economy – the markets, businesses, consumers, and governments – behave.
Macro economics examines economy-wide phenomena such as inflation, price levels, rate of economic growth, national income, GDP and changes in unemployment.

[slide 5]
5
Diff. Between Micro & Macro Economics
Aspect | Micro-economics | Macro-economics
Scope | Studies individual firms and households | Examines the entire economy as a whole
Perspective | Analyses micro-level decisions and markets | Analyses macro-level economy-wide trends
Goals | Investigates market dynamics, prices, and allocation | Aims for overall economic stability, growth and employment
Tools and Analysis | Uses supply and demand, cost-benefit, and utility | Employ national income accounts, monetary policy, and fiscal policy
Policy Implications | Focuses on market-specific policies and regulations | Addresses economy-wide policies, like monetary and fiscal measures

GDP Formula & It’s Impact
GDP = C + I + G + (X-M)
C - here denotes consumption, which includes services, non-durables, and durables
I - denotes the investment expenditure, which consists of spending on housing and equipment
G - represents government expenditure, which includes salaries of employees, construction of roads and railways, airports, schools and spending on the army
( X - M ) - denotes total exports (X) minus total imports (M), is called net exports

A rise in GDP indicates a country’s economy is expanding while
falling GDP rates show an economic contraction.

1. Boost Growth in the Economy
GDP can be increased if there is more Consumption, to accommodate more Consumption there should be more production
To facilitate more production, a company can either use their own capital or borrow it
If borrowing rate is higher than there will be no motivation to do more production
Hence, RBI will decrease the Interest Rate (by reducing Repo Rate) motivating company to do more production

2 – Control Inflation
Inflation means rise in prices of Goods and Services. The prices rise because of high demand among consumers
Consumers demand more because there is high money supply (availability with consumers either owned or owed)
To lower the demand among consumers, the money available should reduce
The RBI will increase the Repo Rate, which will lead to high Interest on Loan and consumer will postpone buying through loan

⬆️ Cash – Move away from risk-assets

Why Do we Need Regulations?
Why Regulations
Industry Regulations and Compliance 3
Why Regulations?
Regulations are crucial in shaping industries and markets, especially in the financial services
sector.
1) Protect Consumer Interests: Regulations protect consumers from unfair practices, fraud, and
exploitation. They ensure that businesses operate transparently and ethically. Examples include
Consumer Protection Laws: Regulations such as the Fair Credit Reporting Act in the U.S.
protect consumers' information and ensure accuracy in credit reporting.
Insurance Regulations: These ensure that insurance companies maintain adequate reserves
to pay out claims, protecting policyholders from the risk of insurer insolvency.
2) Reduce Cost to Consumers: Regulations can help reduce costs for consumers by promoting
competition, efficiency, and fair pricing in the market. They prevent monopolistic behaviors and
price gouging. Examples include
Anti-Trust Laws: These laws prevent monopolies and promote competition, which can lead
to lower prices and better services for consumers.
Utility Regulation: In many places, utilities like electricity & water are regulated to ensure
that prices remain fair & reasonable, preventing companies from charging exorbitant rates.

ty Regulation: In many places, utilities like electricity & water are regulated to ensure
that prices remain fair & reasonable, preventing companies from charging exorbitant rates.
3) Help Consumers Take Informed Decisions: Regulations require companies to provide clear,
accurate, and sufficient information about their products and services, enabling consumers to
make informed choices. Examples include
Disclosure Requirements: Financial institutions are often required to disclose interest rates,
fees, & terms of loans, allowing consumers to compare & choose the best option.
Labelling Standards: Regulations on food labelling ensure that consumers know what
ingredients are in the products they buy and can make healthier choices.

[page 4]
12.1 - Why Do we Need Regulations?
Industry Regulations and Compliance
4) Increase Truth & Faith in the Financial Services Industry: Regulations foster trust by
ensuring that financial institutions operate with integrity and accountability. This increases
consumer confidence in the financial system. Examples include
Auditing Standards: Regulations that require regular, independent audits of financial
institutions ensure accuracy and honesty in financial reporting.
Ethical Conduct Codes: Rules that enforce ethical behavior among financial advisors and
brokers prevent conflicts of interest and fraud.
4
5) Develop the Industry and Markets: Regulations can stimulate the growth and development
of industries and markets by establishing a stable and predictable environment. They provide a
framework within which businesses can innovate and compete. Examples include
Innovation Incentives: Some regulations provide tax breaks or subsidies for research and
development, encouraging innovation within the industry.
Market Regulation: Rules that ensure fair trading practices, such as those implemented by
the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), help develop robust financial markets.
Regulations are essential for maintaining a balance between consumer protection and industry
growth. They ensure that businesses operate fairly and transparently, protect consumers from

ations are essential for maintaining a balance between consumer protection and industry
growth. They ensure that businesses operate fairly and transparently, protect consumers from
unfair practices, provide necessary information for informed decision-making, foster trust in
the financial system, and create an environment conducive to innovation and development.
Summary 
Regulations play a crucial role in ensuring transparency, fairness, and accountability in the
financial system. They protect investors from fraud and mis-selling, ensure proper disclosure of
financial products, and build trust in financial institutions. A well-regulated environment helps
PFPs guide clients with greater confidence and credibility.

Key Objectives of SEBI
Key Aspects
Industry Regulations and Compliance
In India, the securities market is regulated by the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)
under the SEBI Act, 1992. The Act clearly states that SEBI’s purpose is to protect investors,
develop the securities market, and regulate its functioning.
9
Investor Protection
SEBI’s first priority is protecting investors from fraud, mis-selling, false
promises, & unfair practices. It ensures proper disclosures, transparent
communication, & investor education so they can make informed decisions.
Market Regulation
SEBI creates and enforces rules for all stakeholders such as stock exchanges,
listed companies, brokers, mutual funds, and advisors so that the market
functions in an orderly and disciplined manner.
Market Development
SEBI also works on improving the market ecosystem by bringing new
products, better technology, stronger infrastructure, and higher
transparency, making investing easier and more efficient for participants.
Preventing Malpractices
SEBI actively prevents insider trading, price manipulation, circular trading,
and other unfair activities that can harm investors and distort market prices.

Broad Regulatory Areas
Major Regulatory Changes Over a Period
Industry Regulations and Compliance
SEBI regulations for mutual fund distributors (MFDs) cover how schemes are designed,
operated, sold, and monitored so that investors are treated fairly and transparently.
Offer document for schemes: Every scheme must have a Scheme Information Document (SID)
and Key Information Memorandum (KIM) that fully disclose objectives, risks, fees, and other
material details so investors can make informed decisions.
Broad Regulatory Areas
Conversion and consolidation of schemes: Mergers or conversions of schemes require
trustee/board approval and detailed communication to investors, including rationale, impact,
and options to exit without load within a specified window.
New products: AMCs must obtain SEBI approval for new schemes, ensure they are distinct
from existing ones, and follow product specific conditions (e.g., for FoFs, capital protection
funds, REIT/InvIT funds).
Risk management systems: Funds must maintain robust risk management frameworks,
including credit, market, and liquidity risk controls, stress testing, and adherence to internal
limits and SEBI-prescribed norms.
Disclosures and reporting norms: Periodic disclosures of portfolios, scheme performance, risk

controls, stress testing, and adherence to internal
limits and SEBI-prescribed norms.
Disclosures and reporting norms: Periodic disclosures of portfolios, scheme performance, risk
metrics, and material events to investors and SEBI are mandatory, along with half-yearly and
annual reports.
Governance norms: Trustees and AMCs must follow strong governance standards, maintain
proper records, and ensure that schemes are run in the interest of unit holders, with clear
segregation of roles and oversight.

use, etc.) are prescribed to diversify risk and avoid concentration or self-

12.4 - Key SEBI Regulations for MFDs
Industry Regulations and Compliance
Shift from upfront commission to trail commission: Earlier, MFDs used to receive a higher
commission at the time of investment itself. This was changed to trail commission, where
commission is paid gradually as long as the investor continues in the scheme.
Segregated portfolio (side pocketing): In case of credit events in debt or money market
instruments, AMCs can create segregated portfolios so that losses are ring-fenced and
remaining assets continue to be traded fairly.
Performance benchmarking against Total Return Index (TRI): Schemes must benchmark
performance to TRI versions of indices, which include dividends, giving a more realistic
comparison of fund performance.
Valuation of debt and money market securities: SEBI has moved towards market-linked,
matrix-based valuation with common methodologies across AMCs to enhance consistency
and transparency in debt fund NAVs.
Instant access facility: Liquid and money market schemes offering instant redemption must
follow limits on amount and risk controls so that liquidity promises do not endanger
remaining investors.
Restriction on redemption: In exceptional situations (e.g., systemic crises or severe illiquidity),
temporary redemption restrictions may be imposed under SEBI-defined conditions and

striction on redemption: In exceptional situations (e.g., systemic crises or severe illiquidity),
temporary redemption restrictions may be imposed under SEBI-defined conditions and
safeguards to protect investors as a whole.
Distributor due diligence by AMCs: AMCs must conduct ongoing due diligence on
distributors, checking registration, compliance history, mis-selling complaints, and business
practices before and during empanelment.
14
Scheme classification and categorisation: SEBI has standardised scheme categories and
generally permits only one scheme per category per AMC, improving comparability and
reducing clutter for investors.

transparency and investor protection in the mutual fund ecosystem.

Audit requirements: RIAs must undergo an annual compliance audit by a qualified professional
(CA/CS), address any observations, and submit the report to SEBI in the format and timelines
prescribed, demonstrating ongoing adherence to regulations.
Registration with BASL (for RIAs using exchanges/IFSC platforms): Where applicable, RIAs
must also register with BSE Administration and Supervision Ltd. (BASL) or other SEBI
designated supervisory bodies, pay fees, and follow their additional reporting and supervision
framework in addition to SEBI RIA regulations.
RIA Regulation Matrix
The RIA regulation matrix clarifies how financial professionals can offer products and charge
clients under SEBI regulations. It distinguishes between advisory (fee-based) and distribution
(commission-based) models, helping professionals understand where RIAs and non-RIAs are
permitted to operate.

For a RIA, SEBI regulations define eligibility, fee structures, client limits, and strict compliance
requirements to ensure fiduciary responsibility toward clients. RIAs must follow processes such
as risk profiling, suitability assessment, disclosures, record keeping, and grievance redressal while
adhering to a defined code of conduct. These regulations aim to ensure transparency, client

ling, suitability assessment, disclosures, record keeping, and grievance redressal while
adhering to a defined code of conduct. These regulations aim to ensure transparency, client

What is Capital Markets
Types of Capital Markets
9 - Introduction
Capital Markets - Equity & Debt
A capital market is a place where people or institutions with extra money
invest in businesses or governments that need funds. It helps move
money from savers to those who need capital for growth or new
projects.
Secondary Market – This market is where already issued securities are traded between
investors. It provides liquidity and the ability for investors to buy and sell existing
securities.
Primary Market – This is the market where new securities are issued and sold for the first
time. Companies and governments raise new stocks and bonds in this market.
The Three Most Common Capital Markets Are:
Stock Market - The stock market is a public marketplace where shares of
publicly held companies are issued, bought, and sold. It plays a crucial role in
the economy by enabling companies to raise capital through the issuance of
shares to investors.
Bond Market - The bond market, also known as the debt or credit market,
is where participants can issue new debt (in the primary market) or buy
and sell debt securities (in the secondary market). The bond market is
crucial for raising long-term capital.
Currency / Foreign Exchange Market - The foreign exchange market (Forex or
FX) is a global, decentralised market for trading currencies. It is the largest

aising long-term capital.
Currency / Foreign Exchange Market - The foreign exchange market (Forex or
FX) is a global, decentralised market for trading currencies. It is the largest
and most liquid financial market in the world.

[page 4]
Participants of Capital Markets
9 - Introduction
Capital Markets - Equity & Debt
Stock Exchange: Platform for trading securities safely and transparently.
Merchant Bankers: Help companies raise funds and manage public issues.
Investors: Put money into shares or bonds to earn returns.
Stock Brokers: Execute buy and sell orders for investors.
Depositories: Hold securities electronically for safety and easy transfer.
Depository Participants (DPs): Help investors open and manage demat accounts.
Market Regulators (like SEBI): Ensure fair trading and protect investors.
Issuers: Companies or governments that raise money by issuing shares or bonds.

Capital Markets - Equity & Debt
Meaning
For an investor, equity simply means owning a part of a business. By buying equity shares,
the investor receives a share in the company's profits and future growth. Returns from
equity typically come in two forms: periodic dividends declared by the company and capital
appreciation when the share price rises over time. As the business grows and becomes more
valuable, equity investors benefit directly from that expansion.
Market Capitalization Categorization
Meaning
Market capitalization or Market cap, means how much a publicly traded company is worth
based on its total stock value. To calculate the market cap of a company, multiply the
company’s outstanding stock shares by the price of one share. This value determines the level
of market cap. 
Market cap only reflects a company's market value, not its debts or liabilities. Market cap is
useful for determining a company's size, which can indicate a lot about a company's potential
for an investor.
5

[page 6]
Capital Markets - Equity & Debt
To ensure uniformity with respect to the investment universe for equity schemes, SEBI has
decided to define large-cap, mid-cap and small-cap as follows:
Large Cap: Listed companies ranked from 1 to 100 company in the Indian stock
exchanges in terms of market capitalisation
st th
Mid Cap: Listed companies ranked from 101 to 250 in the Indian stock exchanges in
terms of market capitalisation

If a stock is listed on more than one recognised stock exchange, an average of the full

In case a stock is listed on only one of the recognised stock exchanges, the full market
capitalisation of that stock on such an exchange will be considered.
This list would be uploaded on the AMFI website, and the same would be updated every

The data shall be available on the AMFI website within 5 calendar days from the end of the 6

Equity markets, also known as stock markets or stock exchanges, are influenced by a variety of

Economic Growth: Equity markets tend to perform well during periods of strong economic

economy. However, high inflation can erode purchasing power and negatively impact stock
prices.
Monetary Policy: Actions taken by central banks, such as adjusting interest rates or

create uncertainty and volatility in equity markets.

heavily influence stock prices. Factors like confidence, fear, and market sentiment can drive
buying or selling pressure.

sectors, can impact the performance of companies within those sectors and affect equity
markets.
Corporate Actions: Mergers and acquisitions, stock splits, dividend announcements, and
share buybacks can influence stock prices and overall market performance.

economy:
Capital Formation: The stock market lets companies raise money by selling shares

nd

This extra wealth often leads to more spending in the economy.

well-regulated stock market enhances investor trust and confidence, thereby attracting

in the stock market by providing loans, financing IPOs (Initial Public Offerings) and
facilitating stock trading. The performance of the stock market can affect the
financial health of these institutions. For example, during a market downturn,
banks may face a higher risk of non-performing assets (NPAs).

In the Short Term
Market Moves Are Driven by Sentiment and Emotions
Sentiment: Investor mood can quickly push prices up or down, even if fundamentals don’t
change. Market sentiment often shifts due to general optimism or fear. 
Liquidity: More buyers and sellers make it easier to trade stocks and can make markets
move fast. High liquidity usually leads to active price changes and sharp reactions.

prices suddenly. Both good and bad news have strong short-term effects.

Markets are irrational in the short run and can be driven by psychological and situational triggers.
In the Long Term
Market Prices Reflect Business Fundamentals
Profitability: Over time, companies that earn more profit tend to see their stock prices rise.
Investors focus on business growth and financial performance for long-term returns.

Demand & Supply: Stocks go up when more people want to buy than sell, and down when
selling is higher. This basic rule shapes prices over the long run. 
Other Factors: Factors like economic growth, regulations, and technology changes matter
too. Many elements combine to shape equities over years, not just months.
In the long term, stock prices mainly follow how much companies actually earn.
Summary 
As a PFP, the role is to explain that equity markets move due to both macro factors (growth,
interest rates, inflation, policy) and micro factors (earnings, sentiment, liquidity). In the short
term, prices are often driven by news and emotions, so clients must be coached not to react
impulsively. Over the long term, market returns mainly follow business fundamentals and
profit growth, so portfolios should stay aligned with quality companies and suitable risk. The
key is to connect these market realities with each client’s goals and time horizon so they
remain disciplined through volatility.

Understanding Debt Market
What is Debt Market?
Features of Debt Market
Key Terminologies in Debt
Capital Markets - Equity & Debt
What is Debt Market
Meaning
A debt instrument is a legal contract, paper or electronic, through which a borrower raises
money by promising to repay the principal along with periodic interest, enabling issuers to
raise capital in the debt market. It typically pays a fixed or pre-agreed interest to the lender
and repays the principal at maturity, offering predictable cash flows. 
Debt markets are made up of a primary market, where new instruments are first issued to
investors, and a secondary market, where these instruments are later traded among investors
to provide liquidity. Common examples include government securities (G-Secs), corporate and
government bonds, Treasury Bills, debentures, and promissory notes.
Features of Debt Markets
Risk and Return: Debt markets offer a spectrum of instruments, from very safe
government securities to higher-yielding but riskier corporate bonds. Investors trade off
credit quality against return: highly rated issuers usually pay lower interest because
default risk is low, whereas lower-rated issuers must offer higher yields to compensate for
greater chances of delay or non-payment.

default risk is low, whereas lower-rated issuers must offer higher yields to compensate for
greater chances of delay or non-payment.
13
Interest Rate and Yield: Bond prices and interest rates move in opposite directions: when
market interest rates rise, existing bond prices generally fall because their fixed coupons
become less attractive, and vice versa. The yield an investor earns is shaped by current
interest-rate levels, inflation expectations, time to maturity, and the specific terms and
credit risk of the bond.

[page 14]

Diversification: Debt instruments help diversify a portfolio because they often behave
differently from equities, especially during periods of stock-market stress. By adding
suitable debt securities, investors can reduce overall volatility, create more stable income
streams, and better match assets to future liabilities such as EMIs or planned withdrawals.
Issuer: The issuer is usually the Central Government or State government (Government
Securities) or Corporations (Corporate Bonds).
Maturity: The period at the end of which the instrument will be redeemed.
Coupon: A coupon payment is the amount of annual interest that will be paid to the
bondholder on an annual basis. This amount will be paid as per a predefined schedule
– monthly, quarterly, biannually, or annually until the date of maturity.
Calculated As:
Coupon Payment = Face Value of Bond X Coupon Rate of the Bond in %
Face Value: The face value is also known as the par value. Usually, it is the amount paid
back to the investor at maturity.

Introduction to Asset Classes
What is an Asset?
What is an Asset Class?
Asset Classes & Investment Products
Meaning
An asset represents a valuable resource, possessing measurable monetary worth, owned or
controlled by individuals, businesses, or nations. Its significance lies in anticipating future
benefits, as assets are strategically managed to generate returns or contribute to overall
wealth. 
What is an Asset Class?
Meaning
An asset class comprises a group of securities that share similar characteristics and experience
comparable market movements. These securities are typically governed by similar regulations.
Financial experts categorize different investment instruments into distinct asset classes to aid
investors in efficiently diversifying their portfolios.
The careful management and utilization of assets are integral to financial planning and long-
term sustainability, as they are key contributors to economic prosperity and individual financial
well-being. Ultimately, the value of assets extends beyond the present moment, playing a
crucial role in shaping future financial outcomes.
Each asset class varies in terms of risk factors, taxation, return rates, liquidity, tenure, and
market volatility. Consequently, investors often diversify across multiple asset classes to

et class varies in terms of risk factors, taxation, return rates, liquidity, tenure, and

Financial Assets: These are intangible assets you can't touch, like stocks, bonds, and patents.
Their value comes from what they represent, not from the papers themselves. It's important
to note that these papers and certificates themselves have no intrinsic value; they merely
certify ownership and derive their value from the underlying asset.
Physical Assets: Physical assets are tangible, meaning they can be seen and touched, with an
identifiable physical presence. Examples include land, buildings, machinery, tools, equipment,
vehicles, gold, silver, and other tangible economic resources.

Major Asset Classes 
Asset Classes & Investment Products
1) Equity 
Equity represents ownership in a business, obtained by purchasing
shares or stocks that entitle the holder to a claim on profits through
dividends and a residual claim on assets if the company is liquidated
after paying its debts. It is considered a high-risk asset class because
share prices can be very volatile, and company performance or
broader market conditions can lead to both losses and gains. 
At the same time, equity offers high potential returns through capital appreciation and
dividends, making it attractive for investors seeking growth. Listed stocks are generally liquid,
allowing investors to buy and sell quickly without fixed lock-in periods, though actual liquidity
depends on the specific instrument. Because of the higher risk and volatility, equity is most
suitable for long-term investors who can stay invested for many years to aim for returns that
beat inflation.
2) Debt
Debt investments focus on protecting your money and earning regular
income through fixed payments. This includes options like government
bonds, corporate bonds, certificates of deposit, and money market
funds. Debt offers lower risk and less price fluctuation compared to
stocks or equity funds. These investments suit people who want steady
and predictable returns, often including retirees. If held till maturity,

d less price fluctuation compared to
stocks or equity funds. These investments suit people who want steady
and predictable returns, often including retirees. If held till maturity,
debt usually guarantees your interest and repayment of principal. 
Four main risks in debt are interest rate risk, inflation risk, credit risk, and liquidity risk. Your
bond may drop in value if interest rates rise, or your income may lose value if inflation is high.
Corporate bonds add risk if the company cannot pay back the money. Some debt assets may
be hard to sell quickly, causing liquidity risk. Investors seeking higher returns can choose riskier
bonds or longer periods. You can hold debt investments for short, medium, or long terms,
depending on your goals.
10.2 - Types of Asset Classes
5

[page 6]
Major Asset Classes 
Asset Classes & Investment Products
3) Real Estate
Real estate represents ownership of property and is often seen as a
solid, inflation-resistant investment because it is a tangible asset
that can be used or occupied. It can generate returns through rental
income and potential capital appreciation, offering generally
medium-to-high return potential with medium-to-high risk.
Liquidity is lower than equities, since selling a property or finding a
tenant can take time and involves high transaction costs and
ongoing expenses such as maintenance, insurance, and taxes. 
 
Real estate investment trusts (REITs) provide exposure to property income with better liquidity
and lower entry amounts, without directly owning physical property. Overall, real estate suits
long to very long holding periods for investors who can tolerate lower liquidity and higher
upfront and running costs in exchange for relatively steady income and growth potential.
4) Commodities
Gold and silver are widely bought in India not only for cultural and
emotional reasons but also as tangible stores of value that can be
seen, held, and accessed whenever needed. They combine the
characteristics of a precious metal commodity with the role of a
long-term wealth preserver, offering comfort to investors who
prefer assets they can physically verify. Unlike equities or bonds,

s of a precious metal commodity with the role of a
long-term wealth preserver, offering comfort to investors who
prefer assets they can physically verify. Unlike equities or bonds,
these metals are not affected by earnings reports, dividend changes,
or corporate decisions, so fewer external variables influence their
appeal. This simplicity allows gold and silver to continue what they
have done for centuries: help protect purchasing power and act as a
hedge in times of uncertainty.
5) Cash
Cash and cash-equivalent holdings, such as money in savings accounts and other highly liquid
schemes, are part of money market instruments that provide maximum transactional freedom and
instant access. While this offers convenience and safety in nominal terms, returns are usually low
and often fail to keep pace with inflation, gradually eroding purchasing power.

that beat inflation over time while matching each client’s risk tolerance and liquidity needs.

Asset Classes & Investment Products
Equity Investments
Equity – Direct Investments
Listed Equity: These are shares of companies traded on public stock exchanges. Anyone
can buy or sell them easily in the market. Listed equities have clear prices updated daily.
Unlisted Equity: These are shares of private companies not available on public stock
exchanges. They are harder to buy or sell since there is no open market. Pricing is less
transparent and depends on private deals.
ESOPs (Employee Stock Ownership Plan): This allows employees to own shares in the
company they work for. Shares are often given as part of their salary or bonuses. ESOPs
help employees benefit from the company’s growth and profits.
Equity – Managed Portfolio
Equity Mutual Funds: Investors pool their money to buy a wide mix of stocks and bonds.
Fund managers handle buying and selling for everyone. It’s a popular way to get
diversification and professional management

10.3 - Investment Products with Each Asset Class
Asset Classes & Investment Products
PMS (Portfolio Management Services): Professional managers handle individual
investment portfolios for clients. Investments are tailored to client goals and risk levels.
SIFs (Specialized Investment Funds): These are advanced pooled funds using aggressive
strategies. They bridge the gap between mutual funds and PMS/ AIFs. SIFs aim for higher
returns and active management.
Debt Investments
Bank Deposits: Money kept in savings or fixed deposits in banks. Offers safety and steady
but lower interest returns. Easy to access your funds when needed.
Company Deposits: Fixed deposits placed with companies, not banks. Usually offer higher
returns but have more risk. These are less secure if the company has financial trouble.
EPS (Employees’ Provident Fund): Government-managed savings for employees' retirement.
Regular contributions from both employee and employer. Safe with fixed steady returns.
PPF (Public Provident Fund): Long-term government savings scheme with tax benefits. Safe
investment for individuals. Ideal for building a retirement corpus.
Small Savings Schemes: Government-sponsored schemes like SCSS, Post Office & other
schemes. Provide fixed returns and low risk. Suitable for conservative investors.

irement corpus.
Small Savings Schemes: Government-sponsored schemes like SCSS, Post Office & other
schemes. Provide fixed returns and low risk. Suitable for conservative investors.
Bonds: Loans given to governments or companies for a set period. Investors earn regular
interest and get their money back at maturity. Bonds are generally safer than stocks.
Debentures: Debt issued by companies to raise money, usually without collateral. Higher
risk than secured bonds. Pays regular interest to investors.
NCDs: Cannot be converted into shares and are traded on exchanges. Offer fixed income
and are less risky than equities. Maturity dates and interest payments are predetermined.
Debt Mutual Funds: Pooled funds investing in bonds and treasury bills. Aim for stable
returns with low to moderate risk. Managed by professional fund managers.
9
NPS (National Pension Scheme): A government-backed plan for retirement savings in India.
Offers investment options in equity, debt, and government securities. It aims to give steady
income after retirement.
AIFs (Alternative Investment Funds): These are private funds that invest in non-traditional
assets like private equity or real estate. They use unique strategies and are usually meant
for advanced investors. AIFs may have a higher risk or less liquidity.

10.3 - Investment Products with Each Asset Class
Asset Classes & Investment Products
Real Estate Investments
House / Apartment: Residential property for living, owned by individuals or entities. Can
generate rental income and appreciate. A common way for families to build wealth.
Shop / Commercial: Property used for business activities such as retail stores, offices, or
restaurants. Generates income from rents paid by businesses. Popular for those seeking
business-related real estate returns.
Plot of Land: A ground parcel for agricultural or non-agricultural use. Suitable for future
development, farming, or holding as an asset. Land investment may provide long-term
growth.
Real Estate – Physical Investments
REITs (Real Estate Investment Trusts): Companies that own or operate income-producing
real estate. They allow individuals to invest in property without direct ownership. Investors
earn returns from rent and property value gains.
InvITs (Infrastructure Investment Trusts): Trusts owning and running infrastructure projects
like roads and bridges. Investors get a share of the income generated by these projects. InvITs
make it easy to invest in large public assets.
Real Estate PMS: Professional services manage clients’ money in real estate investments.

Gold & Silver ETFs: Exchange-traded funds holding physical gold or silver as assets. Can

Hard Cash or Bank Balance: Actual cash or money kept in a bank account. Ready for

Bars: Gold or silver in bar form, cast or minted in different weights. Often used for

Jewellery: Gold or silver made into ornaments for wearing. Has both decorative and

Investment Risks
Risk comes from not knowing what you're doing
10.4 - Investment Risks
Investment Risks
Four Broad Investment Risks: Volatility, Credit Risk, Illiquidity, Inflation
Risk-Reward of Asset Class
Asset Classes & Investment Products
Volatility - Volatility Risk is the risk of a change of price of a portfolio as a result of changes
in the volatility of a risk factor. It usually applies to portfolios of derivatives instruments,
where the volatility of its underlying is a major influencer of prices.
Credit Risk - Credit Risk is the potential for a lender to lose money when they provide
funds to a borrower. Consumer credit risk can be measured by the five Cs: credit history,
capacity to repay, capital, the loans conditions, and associated collateral. Consumers who
are higher credit risks are charged higher interest rates on loans. Your credit score is one
indicator that lenders use to assess how likely you are to default.
Illiquidity - Illiquidity occurs when a security or other asset that cannot easily and quickly
be sold or exchanged for cash without a substantial loss in value. Illiquid assets may be
hard to sell quickly because of a lack of ready and willing investors or speculators to
purchase the asset, whereas actively traded securities will tend to be more liquid. Illiquid

hard to sell quickly because of a lack of ready and willing investors or speculators to
purchase the asset, whereas actively traded securities will tend to be more liquid. Illiquid
assets tend to have wider bid-ask spreads, greater volatility and as a result, higher risk for
investors.
Inflation - Inflation Risk commonly refers to how the prices of goods and services increase
more than expected. Inversely, such a situation results in the same amount of money
resulting in less purchasing power. Inflation Risk is also known as Purchasing Power Risk.
Charlie Munger

10.4 - Investment Risks
Asset Classes & Investment Products
Summary 
Investment decisions must balance four key risks—volatility, credit, liquidity, and inflation—since
each asset class sits at a different point on the risk–return spectrum. A PFP’s job is to combine
cash, debt, real estate, equity, and commodities so clients get suitable growth, enough liquidity,
and reasonable protection against inflation in line with their risk tolerance and goals.

Qualitative planning often has been dubbed "financial life planning"— or simply "life planning."
It is defined in Michael Kay's book, The Business of Life, as the process of: 
Helping people focus on the true values and motivations in their lives; 
Determining their goals and objectives as they see their lives develop; and 
Using these values, motivations, goals, and objectives to guide the planning process and

Non goal, non product recommendations help clients move closer to their life goals by

Comprehensive Financial Consultancy Process
Monitoring is the ongoing process of regularly collecting and
analysing relevant information to make sure you are doing what you
set out to do. Monitoring a financial plan is essential because it helps
identify potential issues before they become major problems.
Ongoing monitoring allows individuals to make better financial
decisions and gain a better understanding of their financial situation.
Monitoring keeps a financial plan on track by checking whether real life is matching the plan.
Here is a brief elaboration of each technique and strategy.
Regular reviews of financial statements: Periodically analyse income statements, balance
sheets, and cash flow reports to see how spending, saving, assets, and liabilities are evolving.
This highlights leaks, emerging risks, and surplus cash that can be redirected toward goals.
Tracking KPIs and benchmarks: Define key performance indicators such as savings rate, debt-
to-income ratio, or portfolio return versus an index, then track them over time. Comparing
these metrics with appropriate benchmarks shows whether the client is progressing better,
worse, or in line with expectations.

versus an index, then track them over time. Comparing
these metrics with appropriate benchmarks shows whether the client is progressing better,
worse, or in line with expectations.
Comparing actual performance to projections: Match real portfolio values, cash flows, & goal
funding status with the projections made in the financial plan. Any gap between projected &
actual numbers prompts a review of assumptions or behaviour & may require course correction.
17
Assessing progress towards financial goals: Review each goal—such as retirement, education, or
home purchase—to determine what percentage is funded & whether timelines remain realistic.
This keeps clients focused on priorities & helps decide if contributions, risk level, or goal need
adjustment.

Evaluating the impact of external factors: Consider how inflation, tax changes, interest rate
moves, market volatility, or personal life events affect the plan. This allows timely tweaks—like
rebalancing, revising asset allocation, or updating protection cover—so the plan stays resilient.
A Financial plan is dynamic in nature and gets affected by various factors - External & Internal
External Factors
Assumptions about returns, costs, and inflation can
shift with market conditions, requiring updates to
projections, savings rates, or asset allocation.
Changes in tax laws or broader economic and living
conditions (such as recessions, policy changes, or cost
of living shifts) can alter net returns and affordability,
prompting structural tweaks in the plan.
Internal Factors
Variations in income and expenses or changes in job
role, location, or employment status directly affect
surplus cash and risk capacity, demanding a review of
goals and commitments.
Life events—like marriage, divorce, children, evolving
aspirations, unexpected inheritances, or large
unplanned expenses—change priorities and resources,
so goals, timelines, and protections must be revisited
and realigned.

Reviews should be scheduled at regular intervals—typically annually or quarterly—but can
also be conducted whenever significant life or financial changes occur.
This flexibility ensures that the client’s financial plan remains relevant and responsive to
both market conditions and personal circumstances.
Cash Flow: Examine income and expenses to ensure the client is living within their means
and has surplus for investments.
REAL Statement: Review the client’s assets and liabilities to assess net worth and financial
health.
Investments: Evaluate the performance, suitability, and alignment of current investments
with the client’s goals.
Insurance: Check adequacy and relevance of insurance coverage (life, health, property,
etc.).

11.7 - Client Coaching
Client Coaching
Why Coaching?
Behaviour Gap
Potential Obstacles
Comprehensive Financial Consultancy Process
Behavioral Coaching by Personal Financial Professionals (PFPs)
A recent study estimates that an advisor adds about 3% of “advisor alpha” annually within its
own advisor network. That is, working with a financial advisor adds an average of 3% to their
client’s portfolio over time. 
The majority of this value is usually added during periods of heightened greed and fear in the
markets when advisors can step in and help their clients stick with their investment plan, even
when their emotions are driving them to do something else. About one-half of this extra return
comes from the Behavioral coaching that top advisors routinely provide to their clients.
PFP’s who bring a process-oriented approach to their client’s financial plans are helping to
shape their clients’ behaviour. Systematic reviews, periodic rebalancing, proper asset allocation,
and spending plans are all examples of Behavioral coaching. These and other strategies help
clients make financial decisions in an ordered, rational fashion, rather than putting them in a
position to react to news about the stock market or the economy.
21

[page 22]
Client Coaching
A coach is someone who can give correction without causing resentment
John Wooden
11.7 - Client Coaching
Comprehensive Financial Consultancy Process
As a PFP, in any meeting or interaction, if you want to begin with the client, first understand
“why is the client coming to you?” “Why is coaching the client important?” “What are the
various categories of clients? which is very important for you to know whether the client is
coachable or not”
Why is coaching the client important?
The first and most important thing is ‘not everyone is your client’. When you are trying to assess
the segment on which you want to focus more, you take the client in and make sure that not all
of your clients are coachable. You might have taken some of them as your clients due to various
reasons, but they may not be coachable.
So, it is very important to segregate and understand who the clients
are that you want to coach, and you find it difficult to coach. 
There are three categories of clients in terms of client coaching, and
why they become your clients.
Knowledge gap: You will become much more patient with the clients once you sit with them,
they will have many questions for you, and it takes your precious time.
Need handholding.
How they were managing money before they came to you, make them understand the new

h them,

Need handholding.

way of investing because they may not be aware of all the investment avenues.
Don't have time knowledge gap: They don’t have the time; in this case, you just need to coach
the clients so that they can trust you and gain knowledge. And also, to gain confidence in what
you are doing for them.Knowledge gap may or may not be the case, depending on a case-on-
case basis
Hard to coach: Comparing returns with benchmark peers and friends: With this category of
clients, it is quite difficult to make them understand the logic behind the ups and downs of the
market.

[page 23]
Behaviour Gap
11.7 - Client Coaching
Comprehensive Financial Consultancy Process
The clearest evidence of this fact is that investment returns and investor returns are almost
always different. You earn the investment return if you invest your money and then don’t touch
it. No buying, no selling, just holding.
Investor behaviour matters; it probably matters even more than skill.
The bar on the left is noticeably higher than the bar on the right. That’s because most
investors do not have the discipline to stick to their strategies. As a result, they sell when “the
world is ending, and they buy when “this time it is different.
But real people rarely invest this way. Real people chase performance and invest by looking in
the rearview mirror. Markets experience ups and downs. However, over the long term, the
markets have displayed a pronounced upward trend and an incredible degree of resiliency.
Those who have the discipline to stick to their strategy have been rewarded. 
It is precisely the hunt for the best investment that creates a phenomenon called “The
Behaviour Gap, the result of which is well documented. Because of classic behavioural
mistakes, average investors almost always do worse than average investments. 
The topic between you and the big mistake is behavioural finance. The image is brilliant in its

ioural
mistakes, average investors almost always do worse than average investments. 
The topic between you and the big mistake is behavioural finance. The image is brilliant in its
simplicity, even though its underlying message is a complex one. The financial adviser stands
between the client and “The Big Mistake”. But what does that mean?

[page 24]
11.7 - Client Coaching
Comprehensive Financial Consultancy Process
To a large degree, the possibility of these types of mistakes is imaginable and the means of
prevention are also more obvious.
Being a QPFP, you have to be motivated by strategies, not sales. Work with people to identify
the financial risks they are facing and to come up with practical, appropriate, individual
solutions that give them a plan of action and ultimately peace of mind.
It is usually the case that “The Big Mistake” is very hard to fix after it has happened. However,
dealing with a possible problem before it becomes “real” is easy to postpone to some other
time in the future.
However, clients require you as a PFP, if they lack time, knowledge or investment discipline to
avoid the big mistakes.
Some investments are linked to certain goals and the other investments linked to some other
goals. However, all investments would have some or the other goal. If there is no goal, wealth
creation, and upgradation is always there to achieve.
However, there are other financial mistakes that are harder to spot in advance and that may
only reveal themselves much later. Examples of this would be,
Not saving enough to fund your desired income level when you retire,
Choosing not to spend money now on things you enjoy because you are not sure if you can
afford them,

confidence to commit to them.

There would be situations like markets going down then the clients think that we as their PFPs
should have pulled their investments out, during the investing journey there will be troubles
like this but over the longer duration once they start reaching their goals, they will understand.
The obvious Big Financial Mistake is the terrible one,
The major investment that goes bad,
Out-of-control spending and rise in debts, or
Being suddenly unable to work and not having insurance to plug the gap.
24

[page 25]
Potential Obstacles / Deviations
Summary 
Behavioural coaching is one of the biggest value-adds a PFP provides, often worth several
percentage points of extra return by keeping clients invested and disciplined through greed
and fear. Effective PFPs identify which clients are truly coachable, understand whether their
gaps are in knowledge, time, or temperament, and then use structured processes (reviews,
asset allocation, spending plans) to counter common behaviour traps like performance-
chasing, procrastination, and herd mentality. Ultimately, the role is to stand between clients
and “the big mistakes,” focusing on strategies rather than product sales so that clients can
stay on track toward their goals with confidence.

12.1 - Why Set Financial Goals?
Why Set Financial Goals?
12.1
Reasons to set financial goals
Investor Goals & Life Stages
Financial goals are the guiding stars on our journey to financial security and success. They
serve as a roadmap, offering direction and purpose to our financial decisions and actions.
Setting financial goals is a fundamental step in personal finance and can have a profound
impact on your financial well-being. In this article, we will delve into the reasons why setting
financial goals is crucial.
Setting goals provides direction for planning: As a PFP, your role is to help clients define a
clear financial direction. Just like a journey needs a destination, a client’s financial life needs
well-defined goals. Without this, recommendations become product-driven rather than
purpose-driven. Clear goals help you guide clients with intent and keep them accountable
to their financial journey.
Goals define the required savings path: Financial goals enable you to convert aspirations
into numbers. When a client defines a goal, you can calculate how much they need to
invest and by when. Whether it’s a house purchase, child’s education, or retirement, goals
help you move from generic advice to precise, actionable planning.

how much they need to
invest and by when. Whether it’s a house purchase, child’s education, or retirement, goals
help you move from generic advice to precise, actionable planning.
Different goals need different strategies: Not all goals are the same, and as a PFP, your
value lies in designing the right strategy for each. Short-term goals may need safer
instruments, while long-term goals may require growth-oriented investments. Goal-based
planning allows you to tailor solutions and deliver true client-centric advice instead of a
one-size-fits-all approach.
3

[page 4]
Investor Goals & Life Stages
Setting financial goals creates a sense of purpose: As a PFP, your role is not just to
recommend products but to bring meaning to a client’s financial journey. When clients set
goals and achieve milestones—like becoming debt-free or building a retirement corpus—it
creates a sense of progress and trust in your advice. This sense of achievement strengthens
client relationships and reinforces your role as a long-term financial partner.
Goals improve focus and discipline: Clients are constantly exposed to market noise, new
products, and short-term trends. Clear financial goals act as an anchor, helping you guide
clients to stay disciplined and avoid impulsive decisions. As a PFP, you use goals as a filter
to ensure every recommendation aligns with what truly matters to the client.
Goals help shape life decisions: A client’s income is a key driver of their financial plan, and
that often depends on their career choices. As a PFP, when you understand your client’s
financial goals, you can have deeper conversations around career moves, upskilling, or
business decisions. This shifts your role from an investment advisor to a holistic financial
consultant who impacts both income and wealth creation.
Summary 
Setting financial goals is the foundation of a strong and secure financial future. It gives you a

consultant who impacts both income and wealth creation.
Summary 
Setting financial goals is the foundation of a strong and secure financial future. It gives you a
sense of direction, provides a roadmap for your financial journey, and fosters a sense of
accomplishment. Additionally, it helps you remain focused, tailor your financial strategies, and
even influences your career choices. By setting and working toward your financial goals, you're
taking a proactive step toward financial success and well-being.

12.2 - Financial Goal Pyramid
Financial Goal Pyramid
What is Financial Goal Pyramid?
Explanation of Financial Goal Pyramid?
Investor Goals & Life Stages
Financial goals are objectives or milestones that we want our money to achieve in a
particular time frame. Whether it’s building an emergency fund, planning for a vacation,
house reconstruction, children's education, or retirement planning, the key point to note is
that ‘a financial goal needs to be clear’. It’s certainly our duty as PFP to help clients
understand their needs, goals, and the objectives behind setting these goals.
Family financial goals can be viewed as a pyramid, moving step by step from basic “Needs” at
the bottom to “Legacy” at the top, as shown. 
5

[page 6]
Needs - Foundation of the Pyramid
Wants - Improving Quality of Life
Dreams - Aspirations and Life Goals
Investor Goals & Life Stages
Needs are essential expenses that allow a family to live and work, and they usually consume a
major portion of monthly income. These include living expenses, house rent, lifestyle costs,
medical bills, education fees, emergency fund, insurance, and taxes. A PFP first prepares a
detailed expense sheet from the client’s data to understand how much of the income goes
towards these needs. For example, if the monthly income is ₹60,000 and needs a total of
₹40,000, the remaining ₹20,000 can be planned for investments.
Wants sit above needs in the pyramid and are “nice to have” goals that improve lifestyle but are
not necessary for survival. Typical wants include a better house, children’s higher education and
marriage, a comfortable retirement, car purchase, domestic or international vacations, and
home renovation. These goals are often non-recurring and require systematic planning and
disciplined investment to be achieved within a specific time frame. A PFP helps clients
differentiate between needs and wants, reminding them that savings and retirement planning
should be treated as essential, not optional, once basic survival needs are met.
Dreams occupy the next level & reflect higher aspirations such as early retirement, starting a

ning
should be treated as essential, not optional, once basic survival needs are met.
Dreams occupy the next level & reflect higher aspirations such as early retirement, starting a
business, taking a career break, contributing to charity or community, world travel, pursuing
hobbies, or giving meaningful gifts to loved ones. Dreams can also represent feelings like peace
of mind, financial independence, & long-term security. However, dreams alone do not drive
progress unless converted into specific, time-bound financial goals. Example, “I want to retire at
55 with a defined monthly income” is more actionable than “I want to retire early.” A PFP works
with clients to translate these broad dreams into clear targets, investment amounts, & timelines.
12.2 - Financial Goal Pyramid
6
Legacy - Passing Wealth to the Next Generation
Legacy forms the top of the pyramid and focuses on transferring wealth or values to the next
generation or to causes that matter. This includes planning to pass savings to children or
grandchildren, supporting charities, or creating structures that preserve family wealth. Effective
legacy planning starts only after one’s own financial security is ensured, so personal needs,
wants, and dreams are adequately funded. Key estate planning tools include writing a Will to

planning starts only after one’s own financial security is ensured, so personal needs,
wants, and dreams are adequately funded. Key estate planning tools include writing a Will to
clearly record how assets should be distributed and setting up a Trust (such as a family trust) to
manage & pass on assets according to the grantor’s instructions. A PFP can guide clients
through these steps so that legacy goals are realistic, tax-aware, & aligned with family priorities.

[page 7]
Summary 
Financial goals can be organised like a pyramid, starting from basic needs and moving up to
long-term legacy. Needs cover essential living and protection costs, while wants and dreams
focus on improving lifestyle and achieving higher aspirations, such as early retirement or world
travel. As income allows, a PFP helps clients prioritise investments from needs to wants to
dreams. At the top, legacy planning ensures wealth and values are passed efficiently to the next
generation through tools like Wills and Trusts.
Our job is completed when a client achieves their life
goals, not when they invest or buy a financial product

12.3 - Financial Life Stages
Financial Life Stages
The Fulfilment Curve
Financial Life Stages
Irony of Age
Investor Goals & Life Stages
At a certain point, buying more stuff isn’t going to make you feel happy. On the other hand,
particular things you buy absolutely will make life better. This Fulfilment Chart helps you figure
out which is which.
The Fulfilment Curve shows how the satisfaction you get from
spending rises, peaks, and then falls as you spend more
money, just like in the image. At the start, money spent on
survival needs such as food, clothing, and shelter gives a sharp
increase in fulfilment because these are essential to live and
feel secure. As spending moves into “comforts” and then
“luxuries”, fulfilment still rises but at a slower pace, until it
reaches a point called “enough”, where life feels comfortable
and balanced.
Beyond this “enough” zone, extra spending pushes you into overconsumption, where more
purchases actually reduce fulfilment due to higher stress, EMIs, maintenance, and insurance
costs. A bigger house or luxury car may look attractive, but if they force you into a more
stressful job or constant money pressure, you slide down the wrong side of the curve. The key
is to regularly ask, “How much is enough for me?” and then map your own spending on survival,

ul job or constant money pressure, you slide down the wrong side of the curve. The key
is to regularly ask, “How much is enough for me?” and then map your own spending on survival,
comforts, and luxuries to find a personal balance between money spent and genuine fulfilment.
However, it’s tough to describe this for everybody; outlining your own personal purchases and
desires along this chart can be helpful.
8

[page 9]
Financial Life Stages
12.3 - Financial Life Stages
Investor Goals & Life Stages
Financial life stages describe how money decisions evolve from your first pay cheque to
retirement, as shown in the step-style image. Each stage has its own priorities for budgeting,
protection, investing, and debt so that limited income, time, and energy are used wisely.
The First Income Stage
At this stage, the focus is on learning to budget, live within income, and avoid debt traps.
Building an emergency fund and starting basic investments for long-term goals like retirement
are key, even if amounts are small. Health insurance (and other mandatory covers like motor
insurance) is important, while life insurance and estate planning remain optional until you have
dependents.
The Dependent’s Stage
Here, you typically have family members relying on your income, so adequate term life
insurance and expanded health insurance become essential. A realistic budget helps you save
for multiple goals such as children’s education, housing, and retirement, while managing debt
carefully so EMIs do not crowd out key savings. Borrowing is best limited to productive,
wealth-building assets and always within your repayment capacity.
The Growth Stage
Income usually peaks and savings capacity rises in this “golden” phase, making it ideal for

tive,
wealth-building assets and always within your repayment capacity.
The Growth Stage
Income usually peaks and savings capacity rises in this “golden” phase, making it ideal for
accelerating investments towards retirement and other long-term goals. Portfolios should be
reviewed and rebalanced as goals near, and insurance covers updated to reflect higher
responsibilities and assets. With meaningful wealth created, drafting a Will and aligning
nominations with your wishes become important estate-planning tasks.
The Retirement Stage
In retirement, the primary aim is to manage expenses within a relatively fixed income and
protect the retirement corpus from inflation. Investment strategy shifts towards generating
stable income with controlled risk, and adequate health insurance becomes critical because
medical costs can strain finances. Simplifying finances, consolidating accounts, organising
documents, and ensuring all details are updated helps you and your family handle money
matters smoothly in later years.

Across life stages, fulfilment from money rises sharply when basic survival and comfort needs
are met, then flattens at the “enough” point before falling with overconsumption. At the same
time, time, money, and energy are never all abundant together. Youth have time and energy,
adulthood has money and energy, and old age has time and money, which makes planning
crucial. A Personal Finance Professional (PFP), therefore, helps clients spend right and invest
right at each stage from first income to retirement, so limited resources create maximum,
sustainable fulfilment.
