Asset Allocation Models & Consultancy 6
22.1 - Asset Allocation & Diversification
Correlation measures how two assets move in relation to each other. The lower the correlation
— the more they protect each other in a portfolio.
The Three Levels of Correlation
Correlation = +1 (Move Together Always — No Diversification)
When two assets move in the same direction, by the same magnitude, at the same time, they
offer no diversification benefit. Holding both is essentially the same as holding one — the risk
does not reduce, it simply gets split across two names.
Correlation = 0 (Move Independently — Diversification)
When two assets have no relationship with each other's movements, combining them begins to
reduce overall portfolio risk. When one falls, the other is unaffected — which cushions the
portfolio from concentrated losses.
Correlation = -1 (Move in Opposite Directions — Optimum Diversification)
When two assets move in perfectly opposite directions, combining them delivers the maximum

entrated losses.
Correlation = -1 (Move in Opposite Directions — Optimum Diversification)
When two assets move in perfectly opposite directions, combining them delivers the maximum
possible risk reduction. In theory, a perfectly balanced portfolio of two such assets could
eliminate risk entirely — though in practice, perfect negative correlation rarely exists across full
market cycles.
For a PFP, correlation is the tool that separates genuine diversification from the illusion of it.
The goal in asset allocation is not simply to hold many assets — it is to hold assets whose
correlations with each other are as low as possible, so that the portfolio as a whole remains
stable even when individual components are under stress.

[page 7]
Asset Allocation Models & Consultancy 7
22.1 - Asset Allocation & Diversification
Holding large cap, mid cap, and small cap equity funds together may feel diversified, but all
three move broadly in the same direction when Indian equity markets rise or fall. During the
March 2020 COVID crash, all three categories fell sharply together. The diversification benefit
is limited because the underlying driver — equity market sentiment — is the same for all three.
High Positive Correlation (+1)
Equity and debt respond differently to the same economic events. When RBI cuts rates, debt
prices rise while equity markets may react mixed. When equity markets rally strongly, debt
returns remain steady and unaffected. Combining the two in a portfolio creates a better risk
balance — smoothing out the sharp swings that a pure equity portfolio would experience.
Low Correlation (0)
Gold, long-duration G-Secs, international equity funds, and REITs all tend to move
independently of or opposite to equity markets. Each is driven by a different set of economic
triggers — currency movements, interest rate cycles, global growth, or rental income — rather
than market sentiment. This means when equity falls sharply, these asset classes are either
unaffected or move in the opposite direction, providing a natural counterweight. The result is

arket sentiment. This means when equity falls sharply, these asset classes are either
unaffected or move in the opposite direction, providing a natural counterweight. The result is
downside protection at the portfolio level during periods of market stress.
Negative Correlation (-1)
Why Asset Allocation is Important?
Different asset classes behave differently over time because each has its own risk and
return pattern, so combining them can reduce the overall portfolio’s price ups and downs.
Holding multiple asset classes in one portfolio reduces the impact if any one asset
performs poorly, thereby lowering overall risk and volatility.
Each financial goal (like buying a house, children’s education, retirement) needs a different
mix of assets based on time horizon and risk profile.
Different asset classes are taxed differently in India, so the chosen allocation can change
an investor’s post-tax and real returns.

Summary 
Asset allocation is the process of distributing investments across asset classes like equity,
debt, gold, and others to balance risk and return as per goals, time horizon, and risk profile.
Diversification means spreading investments within or across those classes to reduce risk. A
well-planned mix helps manage volatility, improve stability, and enhance long-term returns,
though investors often face challenges like misjudging risk tolerance, emotional decisions, and
poor rebalancing or over-diversification.

[page 9]

Factors to Consider for Asset Allocation
Individual's Goals:
Every client has a different set of financial goals — a child's
education, home purchase, retirement, or wealth creation. The
nature of each goal — its size, priority, and flexibility — directly
shapes how the portfolio needs to be structured to fund it.
22.2 - Asset Allocation Process & Approach
Asset Allocation Process & Approach
22.2
Factors to Consider for Asset Allocation
Asset Allocation Process
Asset Allocation Approach
Asset Allocation Models & Consultancy 9
Investment Horizon:
How long a client has before they need the money determines
how much risk the portfolio can carry. A goal that is 20 years
away can absorb short-term market volatility; a goal that is 2
years away cannot. Short, medium, and long-term goals within
the same client's life may each require a different allocation.
Risk Profile:
A client's risk profile captures both their ability to take risk
(income stability, liabilities, dependents) and their
willingness to take risk (emotional comfort with market
fluctuations). Two clients with identical goals and horizons
may need different allocations if their risk profiles differ.

[page 10]
Asset Allocation Models & Consultancy 10
1
Establishing Goals, Timeline & Risk Profile:
The first step in the asset allocation process is to determine the investor's goals,
such as saving for retirement, vacation, house purchase, startup or a child's
education, and their risk profile. Risk profile refers to an investor's willingness and
ability to tolerate risk.
2
Identifying Asset Classes:
The next step is to identify the different asset classes that will be included in the
portfolio. Common asset classes include equity, debt, cash, real estate, and gold.
3
Determining Target Allocation:
After identifying the asset classes, the next step is to determine the target
allocation for each asset class. This is based on the investor's risk profile and
financial goals.
4
Selecting & Allocating Specific Investments:
Once the target allocation for each asset class has been determined, the investor
must select specific investments to include in the portfolio. For example, if the
target allocation for the equity portion of the portfolio is 60%, then PFP choose to
invest in individual stocks or exchange-traded funds (ETFs) or mutual fund.
5
Monitoring and Rebalancing:
Finally, the PFP must monitor the portfolio's performance and periodically rebalance
the portfolio to maintain the target asset allocation. Rebalancing involves buying

Rebalancing:
Finally, the PFP must monitor the portfolio's performance and periodically rebalance
the portfolio to maintain the target asset allocation. Rebalancing involves buying
and selling assets to bring the portfolio back to its target allocation.
Overall, the asset allocation process is a critical component of investing, and it requires careful
consideration of an investor's goals, risk profile, and asset allocation strategies. By following a
disciplined approach to asset allocation, PFPs can balance risk and return and achieve client
financial goals.

Approach 1 - Age Based
The age-based approach works on the principle that as a client gets older, their capacity to
absorb market volatility reduces and the portfolio should progressively shift from equity to debt.

Approach 3 — Goal Based
This approach determines allocation based on how far away the goal is. The closer the goal, the

Choosing the Right Approach
The goal-based approach is the most complete of the three — it incorporates the client's risk
profile, time horizon, and specific financial goals into every allocation decision. The final allocation
must always be anchored to the client's goals.
Age-based allocation is simple but ignores goals and risk profile. Risk profile-based allocation
captures the client's temperament but misses the timeline. Goal-based allocation brings all three
dimensions together — making it the most robust framework for building a client's portfolio.

Asset Allocation Models & Consultancy 13
Asset allocation strategies describe how a portfolio mix is decided and changed over time, not
just what percentage goes into each asset class. PFPs should understand these strategies
conceptually and then choose what suits their approach.
Strategic Asset Allocation is a long-term approach where a fixed
allocation ratio is set for the portfolio and maintained consistently
over time, regardless of short-term market movements.
Fixed Asset Allocation
A specific equity-to-debt ratio is decided upfront based on the client's goals, horizon, and risk
profile — and this ratio becomes the portfolio's target. For example, a 60:40 equity-to-debt split
is set and held as the baseline, irrespective of what markets do in the interim.
Periodic Rebalancing
Over time, market movements cause the actual allocation to drift from the target. If equity
markets rally strongly, the equity portion may grow to 70% — moving the portfolio away from
the intended 60:40 split. Periodic rebalancing corrects this drift by selling the over-weighted
asset class and adding to the under-weighted one, restoring the original ratio.
Rebalancing Trigger

asset class and adding to the under-weighted one, restoring the original ratio.
Rebalancing Trigger
In strategic allocation, the trigger for rebalancing is time-based, not market-based. The portfolio
is reviewed and rebalanced at pre-defined intervals — annually or semi-annually — regardless of
whether markets are up, down, or flat at that point.

Tactical Asset Allocation
22.3 - Asset Allocation Strategies
Asset Allocation Models & Consultancy 14
Investment Discipline
Because rebalancing happens on a fixed schedule rather than in reaction to market events, this
strategy removes emotion from the process. The portfolio is not adjusted every time markets
move — only when the review date arrives. Annual rebalancing is the standard recommendation
under this approach.
Example of Moderate Risk Profile Client Portfolio:
In the example, the initial strategic mix for a moderate investor is 60% equity and 40% debt. After
one year, equity grows faster, and the mix drifts to 65% equity and 35% debt, so the PFP simply sells
5% of equity and buys 5% of debt to bring the allocation back to the original 60:40 level, thereby
rebalancing the portfolio with the recommended client portfolio.
Tactical Asset Allocation is a flexible approach where the equity-
to-debt ratio is temporarily adjusted based on short-term market
conditions, with the intention of capitalising on emerging
opportunities or reducing risk during unfavourable periods.

opportunities or reducing risk during unfavourable periods.
Flexible Asset Allocation
Unlike strategic allocation which holds a fixed ratio, tactical allocation allows the portfolio mix
to shift in response to market conditions. If equity markets appear favorable, the equity
proportion is increased; if conditions look uncertain, it is reduced in favor of debt.
Momentum-Based Strategy
This approach depends on the ability to read and anticipate short-term market movements. The
allocation changes are not calendar-driven but are based on market signals — making it an
active, judgment-led strategy rather than a passive, rule-based one.

[page 15]
22.3 - Asset Allocation Strategies
Asset Allocation Models & Consultancy 15
Tactical Adjustment
The adjustment is a temporary deviation from the base allocation. For example, a portfolio
running at 60% equity and 40% debt may be shifted to 80% equity and 20% debt when market
conditions look favorable — and then returned to the original mix once the opportunity has
played out or the risk environment changes.
Pre-Decided Base Allocation
Despite its flexibility, tactical allocation is not unconstrained. A base allocation is always pre-
decided, and all tactical shifts are deviations from that base — not a complete departure from it.
The base allocation continues to reflect the client's long-term goals and risk profile.

Dynamic Asset Allocation
Dynamic Asset Allocation is a market-responsive strategy where
the equity-to-debt ratio continuously shifts based on market
movements — with no fixed allocation ratio as the anchor.
Market-Responsive
The portfolio adjusts its equity and debt exposure in direct response to market direction. When
markets are rising, equity exposure is increased; when markets are falling, the portfolio shifts
towards debt. Alternatively, the opposite approach — buying equity when markets fall and
reducing it when markets rise — is used to buy low and sell high systematically.

Flexible Approach
Unlike tactical allocation which deviates temporarily from a pre-set base, dynamic allocation
operates without fixed percentages altogether. The allocation at any point is entirely
determined by market conditions and the underlying model — making it the most fluid of the
three strategies.
When to Use
This strategy is most suitable when a systematic, model-driven allocation framework is in place
— where allocation decisions are guided by valuation indicators, market signals, or a rules-based
model rather than by individual judgment or a fixed schedule.

Rebalancing is the process of adjusting the portfolio's asset allocation back to its original target
allocation. This is typically done by buying or selling assets to bring the portfolio back to its
target allocation.
What is Rebalancing?

Strategies for Rebalancing
Why Rebalancing is Necessary?
Asset Allocation Models & Consultancy 18
Time-Based Strategy:
Rebalancing at fixed intervals (for example, quarterly, semi-annually or annually),
regardless of how much weights have moved.
Threshold-Based Strategy:
Rebalancing is triggered only when an asset allocation deviates from its target allocation
by certain percentage.
Hybrid Strategy:
Combines both methods by checking the portfolio at fixed times and rebalancing only if
deviations are beyond defined thresholds, balancing discipline with cost control.
Note: Before rebalancing, PFPs should consider whether the method of rebalancing will trigger
transaction fees or tax consequences. We cover tax implications of each asset class in detail in Topic
- Capital Gains Tax
Asset allocation naturally changes as different asset classes grow at different speeds, and this
change can silently shift a client from a moderate to an aggressive or conservative risk
position without any conscious change. Regular rebalancing is therefore essential to bring the
allocation back in line with the agreed risk profile and goal plan, so that the client is not
unknowingly exposed to higher risk than they can handle, or stuck in a conservative allocation
that may not meet long-term objectives.

22.4 - Understanding Portfolio Rebalancing

[page 19]
Mistakes To Avoid
Asset Allocation Models & Consultancy 19
22.4 - Understanding Portfolio Rebalancing
Without a defined investment strategy, portfolio decisions become reactive and
inconsistent — every market movement triggers a different response with no clear
rationale holding it together.
Agreeing on a strategy and then abandoning it during market stress defeats the entire
purpose — the strategy was built precisely for moments when staying the course feels
uncomfortable.
Chasing NFOs, thematic funds, or trending sectors because they are generating buzz leads
to a portfolio built on noise rather than the client's actual goals and risk profile.
Deciding the equity-debt split is only half the job — within each asset class, concentration
in a single fund, sector, or instrument still leaves the portfolio exposed to avoidable
specific risk.
A client's allocation that was right at age 35 will not be right at age 50 — life stages,
income changes, and proximity to goals all demand that the allocation is reviewed and
adjusted over time.
A job change, an inheritance, a new dependent, or a shifted retirement timeline all change
what the portfolio needs to do — failing to revisit these circumstances means the portfolio
may be optimised for a life the client no longer lives.

● 20/05/21 - ₹ 20,000
● 14/06/22 - ₹ 25,000

Find the returns generated by Ram?
A5=3 · B5=Priyanka, QPFP® is planning to recommend ₹ 2.5 crores life insurance cover to her client Ajay Bansal aged 35. Ajay's spouse is a home-maker. He currently bought his own house for which he took a loan for ₹50,00,000. As he is highly qualified he also wants her daughter to study abroad. The present value of the higher education is coming around ₹20,00,000. His household & lifestyle expenses are ₹ 5,00,000 and ₹ 2,00,000 respectively.

Following are the assumptions which Priyanka took while calculating the life insurance requirement:

● Discounting Factor: 10%
● Remaining life expectancy of spouse: 50 years
● Inflation rate on expenses: 6%
● Tax on investment income: 10%
● Expected investment returns on insurance proceeds: 10%
● Existing assets: ₹50,00,000 | Existing Term Plan: ₹50,00,000

Should Priyanka go ahead and recommend ₹2.5 crores life insurance to her client?
A6=4 · B6=Prathamesh is planning to buy a house which is costing ₹ 80,00,000 as of today. Based on past data the additional cost that one incurs after buying a house is 15% and the real estate inflation is expected at around 6%.

As he has more financial commitments, he is planning to buy a house after 8 years once his son's primary education is completed. He is planning to sell his current house at around ₹ 50,00,000 after 8 years. Assuming 12% returns for the SIP, 50% loan funding for the same, what SIP will be needed to accumulate the corpus for the down-payment & additional cost after 8 years?

25.1
Parties Associated with Life Insurance Policies
Insurer - The insurer is the life insurance company. It accepts risk, issues the policy,
collects premium and pays the claim as per the contract.
Insured - The insured is the person whose life is covered under the policy. If this person
dies or survives, depending on product design, the contractual benefit becomes payable.
Policy Holder - The policyholder is the person who owns the policy and pays the premium.
The policyholder and the insured can be the same person or different (for example, parent
as owner and child as insured).
Nominee - The nominee is the person named by the policyholder to receive the policy
money from the insurer if the insured dies during the policy term. Nominees are usually
close family members such as spouse, children or parents and must submit a claim to the
insurer.
Beneficiary - A beneficiary is any person or entity that ultimately benefits from the policy
proceeds. In many cases, nominee and beneficiary are the same, but in some situations
such as, certain legal disputes or trusts they can differ.
25.1 - Terms Associated with Life Insurance
Terms Associated with Life Insurance
Parties Associated with Life Insurance Policies

Parties Associated with Life Insurance Policies
Life Insurance Policies Terms
Life Insurance Products 4
For example, Rohit buys a life insurance policy on his own life. In
the proposal form he writes his wife Meera as nominee, so the
insurer will pay the death claim to Meera if Rohit dies. If Rohit’s
Will says that this policy money finally belongs to their two
children, then Meera is only the nominee (she receives the money
from the insurer and holds it), while the beneficiaries in law are
the two children, who will receive the money as per the Will.

[page 5]
Life Insurance Policies Terms
Premium - An insurance premium equates to the money that is paid by any person or
company / business for availing of an insurance policy. The insurance premium amount is
influenced by multiple factors and varies from one payee to another.
Sum Assured - A sum assured is a fixed amount that is paid to the nominee of the plan in
the unfortunate event of the policyholder’s demise. The insurance company pays this
money as per the sum chosen by one at the time of purchasing the policy.
Underwriting - Underwriting is the process by which the insurer evaluates the risk of each
proposal. The underwriter studies details such as age, income, medical history, occupation
and lifestyle and then decides whether to accept the risk, at what terms and at what
premium.
Free Look Period - Free-look period is the time allowed to a new policyholder to review
the policy terms after receiving the document. If the person is not satisfied, they can
return the policy within 15 or 30 days (as specified) and get the premium back after
deducting expenses like stamp duty and medical costs.
Premium Paying Term (PPT) - PPT is the number of years for which the policyholder has to
pay premiums. It can be the same as the policy term or shorter (for example, pay for 10
years, cover for 20 years). Premiums are usually paid monthly, quarterly, half-yearly or

to
pay premiums. It can be the same as the policy term or shorter (for example, pay for 10
years, cover for 20 years). Premiums are usually paid monthly, quarterly, half-yearly or
yearly; some policies allow a single premium also.
Policy Tenures - Policy term is the length of time for which life cover is provided under the
policy. During this period, premiums are payable as per PPT and the insurer is on risk; if
the insured dies within this term, benefits are paid according to the policy.
Exclusions - Exclusions are specific situations or circumstances mentioned in the life
insurance policy where the insurance company may not provide coverage or pay out
benefits.
As per IRDAI's latest regulations (Master Circular 2024), all life insurance policies with a
term of one year or more now offer a uniform 30-day free look period.
25.1 - Terms Associated with Life Insurance
Life Insurance Products 5
Common exclusions include death due to suicide within the first 12 months after policy
issuance, participation in hazardous activities, or pre-existing health conditions, depending
on the policy terms.

[page 6]
Claim - A claim in the context of life insurance refers to the formal request made by the
policyholder or their beneficiaries to the insurance company to receive the benefits
specified in the policy. This request is typically made in the event of the policyholder's
death or when the policy matures.
Maturity/ Survival Benefits - Maturity benefit or survival benefit is the amount payable to
the policyholder if they survive the entire policy term. It is the lump sum amount that the
insurance company pays out to the policyholder upon the maturity of the policy.
Death Benefit - The Death Benefit is the amount paid to the nominee if the policyholder
dies during the policy term. It may include the sum assured and other additions like
bonuses or rider benefits.
Surrender Value - If the policyholder decides to end the policy before maturity, the insurer
may pay a Surrender Value. This value depends on how long the policy has been active and
the number of premiums paid. Not all policies carry a surrender value, especially in early
years.
Grace Period - If one couldn’t pay the renewal premium for their policy on time, the life
insurance company gives them an extension in the number of days after the premium
payment due date. A ‘Grace Period’ can be a period of 15 days in case of monthly premium
payment mode and 30 days in case of quarterly, half-yearly and annual premium payment

emium
payment due date. A ‘Grace Period’ can be a period of 15 days in case of monthly premium
payment mode and 30 days in case of quarterly, half-yearly and annual premium payment
mode.
Paid Up Value – A life insurance policy becomes ‘paid-up’ when the policyholder decides
to stop paying premiums after a certain period. As per recent regulations, if the
policyholder stops paying the premium amount after they have paid the premium for at
least a year, the policy automatically converts to reduced paid-up status. The policy then
continues with a reduced sum assured, known as the paid-up value.
25.1 - Terms Associated with Life Insurance
Life Insurance Products 6
However, during the grace period the risk cover continues. If death occurs, the insurer still
pays the death benefit but deducts any unpaid premium.
Term plans and ULIPs do not qualify for this feature.

Revival - The revival period is the span of time offered by the insurance company during
which the policyholder can reactivate a lapsed policy. Once the revival period is over the
policy can never be re-activated even if the policyholder wants to pay all the premium
payments that are due.
25.1 - Terms Associated with Life Insurance
Life Insurance Products 7
Lapse occurs fully in term plans & ULIPs with no paid-up feature, losing all protection and
past premiums
Lapsed Policy - If premiums are not paid even after the grace period ends and eligibility for
paid-up is not met, the policy can lapse. To put it simply, it means that the life insurance
contract between the insured and the insurer will become inactive. The policyholder and
their family will no longer be entitled to receive life coverage or insurance policy benefits
in case of a lapsed policy.
Summary 
In summary, life insurance involves key parties like insurer, insured, policyholder, nominee, and
beneficiary, alongside essential terms such as premium, policy term, sum assured,
underwriting, free look period, exclusions, claims, maturity/death benefits, surrender value,
grace period, paid-up value, lapsed policy, and revival.
These elements ensure clear risk transfer, policy management, and claim settlement for
policyholders.
Understanding them helps families secure financial protection effectively.

As a personal finance professional, here the first question to make the clients understand is,
Why life insurance before investments?
Life insurance protects family income if the main earner dies suddenly. It comes before
investments because savings alone cannot replace decades of lost earnings. Investments may
lose value if sold under pressure after death.
A family requires immediate liquidity to cover ongoing expenses like rent, groceries, and school
fees. Even top investments cannot match 30 years of future income. Only life insurance fills
this gap effectively.
It is only a life insurance plan that provides adequate life insurance coverage that can help and
fill the space. It is here that a life insurance plan is ideal to have.
There are five major types of life insurance –
Term Plan
Endowment Plan
Money-back Plan
Whole Life Policy
Unit Linked Insurance Plan (ULIP)

[page 9]
Term Insurance Plan
25.2 - Types of Life Insurance
Life Insurance Products 9
Term insurance is a pure life cover that pays a lump sum to the
nominee if the insured person dies during the policy term. It is widely
used in India as the pure protection for a family’s long-term financial
security & is usually the first life insurance product a Personal Finance
Professional (PFP) recommends while designing a protection plan.
Pure Protection - Term insurance is a pure protection plan that pays a fixed sum assured
only if the insured person dies during the chosen term of the policy; there is no maturity
value if the person survives the term.
No Savings Element - Term insurance does not build cash value or maturity value; the
entire premium goes towards risk cover and charges. Over the last 15–20 years, this “no
savings” structure has allowed insurers in India to price term plans competitively and offer
higher covers compared to traditional endowment or money-back policies.
Economical Coverage - Premiums are comparatively low because there is no savings or
investment element, making term insurance a cost-effective way for families to secure a
large cover during high-responsibility years such as loan repayment & children’s education.
Fixed-Term Coverage - Provides cover for a defined term (e.g 20–40 years); once the term

large cover during high-responsibility years such as loan repayment & children’s education.
Fixed-Term Coverage - Provides cover for a defined term (e.g 20–40 years); once the term
ends, cover stops unless renewed or a new policy is purchased as per policy conditions.

[page 10]
Variations Available - Life insurance companies offer different term structures such as level
term, decreasing term, and increasing term.
25.2 - Types of Life Insurance
Life Insurance Products 10
Level term - Sum assured remains constant throughout the policy term; this is the
most common option recommended for meeting long-term family protection needs.
Decreasing term - Sum assured reduces at a pre-decided rate, often aligned with a
loan outstanding; suitable where the primary objective is to protect a specific liability
such as a home loan.
Increasing term - Sum assured rises at a defined rate to broadly keep pace with
inflation and growing responsibilities; premiums are usually higher than level term for
the same initial cover.
Fixed Premium Structure - The premium is locked in at policy inception based on the
insured's age, health, and lifestyle at that point, and remains unchanged for the entire term.
Flexible Payout Options - The death benefit can be structured as a one-time lump sum, a
monthly income stream, or a combination. This is especially useful for families where the
nominee may not be equipped to manage a large corpus responsibly.
Common Riders - A rider is an optional add-on to a life insurance policy that provides extra
protection for an additional premium. Common riders such as accidental death benefit,

.
Common Riders - A rider is an optional add-on to a life insurance policy that provides extra
protection for an additional premium. Common riders such as accidental death benefit,
disability and critical illness can be added for extra protection.
Income Replacement - Term insurance is designed to replace the economic value of the life
assured for the financial dependents left behind. The death benefit effectively substitutes
the future income stream that ceases upon the policyholder's demise, ensuring the
family's financial obligations remain funded.
Coverage Flexibility - Policyholder can choose the sum assured, policy term, and premium
payment term independently based on their income and protection needs. For example, a
self-employed professional may opt for a limited pay option to finish premiums early while
keeping cover active longer.

[page 11]
Death and Maturity Benefits - Endowment policies pay the sum assured plus applicable
bonuses to the nominee on the life assured’s death during the term, and a maturity value if
the policyholder survives the full term. This dual benefit helps Indian families combine
protection with planned savings for future financial goals.
Bonus Inclusions
25.2 - Types of Life Insurance
Life Insurance Products 11
These plans do not
participate in insurer’s
profits. All benefits are
pre-defined and
guaranteed.

Survival Benefits - If all premiums are paid and the policy term completed, the policyholder
receives a guaranteed maturity amount, often enhanced by bonuses. This survival benefit
supports long-term goals such as children’s higher education or home purchase.
Under participating endowment plans, a PFP generally encounters three main bonuses:
Reversionary (simple/compound) bonus – Declared periodically and added to the sum
assured, becoming guaranteed once added.
Interim bonus – A pro-rata bonus given for the period since the last declared bonus if a
claim or maturity happens before the next declaration.
Terminal (loyalty) bonus – A one-time bonus paid at maturity or death to reward

the period since the last declared bonus if a
claim or maturity happens before the next declaration.
Terminal (loyalty) bonus – A one-time bonus paid at maturity or death to reward
long-term policyholders, based on insurer performance and policy duration.
Endowment Insurance Plan
An endowment insurance plan is a life insurance policy that combines
risk cover with a savings element. In India, such plans have been used
for many years by households that prefer stable, low-risk returns
rather than market-linked volatility and want a fixed amount at a
specific future date for children’s education, marriage or retirement.

[page 12]
Long-Term Commitments - Policyholder must stay invested & pay premiums regularly for
the entire policy term to receive full benefits. If policy is structured for long durations, so
breaking it early usually reduces benefits & may lead to lower values. To get optimum
maturity or death benefits, the policyholder must remain committed to the policy term.
25.2 - Types of Life Insurance
Life Insurance Products 12
Loan Facility - A loan facility under an endowment insurance plan allows the policyholder
to borrow against the policy’s surrender value once the policy has run for a minimum
period and has acquired cash value. The policy is temporarily assigned to the insurer or
lender as security until the loan is repaid. Most Indian insurers typically allow a loan of
about 70%–90% of the surrender value.
The exact terms & conditions are defined in each product brochure and vary from insurer
to insurer, which a Personal Finance Professional (PFP) must check before advising clients.
Limited Liquidity - Endowment policies are not designed for frequent withdrawals, and
surrendering early usually leads to low surrender values and loss of bonuses.
Money Back Plan
Money Back policy is a type of an endowment plan only. The unique
feature of this policy is, it provides for a percentage of sum assured at
regular intervals (called survival benefits), instead of getting the lump

endowment plan only. The unique
feature of this policy is, it provides for a percentage of sum assured at
regular intervals (called survival benefits), instead of getting the lump
sum amount at the end of the term. The remaining amount along with
the bonus is paid at policy maturity.
However, if the policyholder dies during the policy tenure, the full sum assured is paid to the
nominee regardless of the survival benefits already paid.
Death & Maturity Benefits - The plan combines savings with life cover, paying the full sum
assured to the nominee upon death regardless of survival benefits already paid out. On
maturity, the policyholder receives the remaining corpus along with any accrued bonuses.
Riders Available - Common riders with endowment policies are accidental death benefit,
critical illness, disability and waiver of premium. These add extra protection layers.
Higher Premium, Lower Coverage - Because part of each premium goes into savings,
endowment plans charge higher premiums than term insurance for the same sum assured.
As a result, Indian policyholders often have modest life cover from endowment policies
and may need additional term cover for adequate protection.
Non-Participating Plans - Non-participating endowment plans do not share in the insurer’s
profits, so they generally do not earn bonuses and instead offer only the guaranteed

tion.
Non-Participating Plans - Non-participating endowment plans do not share in the insurer’s
profits, so they generally do not earn bonuses and instead offer only the guaranteed
benefits specified in the policy.

Remaining 40% of sum assured at maturity in the 20th year.
These four “money-back” instalments together add up to 100% of the sum assured, and the
policy continues with full life cover throughout the term, even after earlier instalments are paid.
If the life assured dies at any time during the 20-year term, the nominee receives the Sum
Assured on Death along with accrued Simple Reversionary Bonuses and any Final Additional
Bonus, subject to policy terms.
At maturity, if the life assured survives and premiums are paid up to date, the policy pays the
last money-back instalment of 40% of sum assured plus vested Simple Reversionary Bonuses
and any Final Additional Bonus, after which the policy terminates.
Periodic Returns - Money back plans provide regular payouts at fixed intervals as a
pre-defined percentage of the sum assured while the policyholder is alive and the policy is
in force. These regular payouts give liquidity for recurring needs like school fees or EMIs,
instead of receiving the entire amount only at maturity.

in force. These regular payouts give liquidity for recurring needs like school fees or EMIs,
instead of receiving the entire amount only at maturity.
Survival Benefits - If the life assured survives the complete policy term, the remaining
maturity benefit (sum assured minus survival payouts already received) along with
accumulated bonuses is paid out. This ensures the policyholder is not left with nothing
simply because they received interim payouts along the way.

[page 14]
Matured Endowment Benefits - If the insured person survives to the age (for example 99
or 100), whole life plans pay a lump-sum maturity amount similar to a matured
endowment. This amount may include the basic sum assured and any accrued bonuses.
Lifetime Coverage - These policies provide life cover as long as the policy remains in force,
usually until age 99 or 100, subject to premium payment conditions. For Indian families,
this means the nominee is eligible for the sum assured whenever death occurs during this
long period, which can be useful for lifelong dependents.
Common Premium Options
Limited premium whole life - Premiums are paid only for a fixed, shorter period (for
example 10–20 years), while coverage continues up to 99–100 years.
Convertible whole life policy - Some policies allow conversion from an endowment or
any other plan into a whole life policy at specified times, subject to policy rules.
25.2 - Types of Life Insurance
Life Insurance Products 14
Single premium whole life - One-time lump-sum premium at inception, after which the
policy stays in force for the whole life without further payments.
Continuous/regular premium whole life - Premiums are paid periodically (yearly,
half-yearly, etc.) throughout life or for a long duration, with level payments.
Whole Life Insurance Policy

ous/regular premium whole life - Premiums are paid periodically (yearly,
half-yearly, etc.) throughout life or for a long duration, with level payments.
Whole Life Insurance Policy
Extended Maturity - Whole life policies work like an endowment plan but with a very long
maturity age, commonly 99 or 100 years of insured. Because of this extended term, the
policy can support legacy planning, as benefits are typically received either on earlier
death or on reaching the maturity age.
Whole life insurance is a life policy that provides coverage for almost
the entire lifetime of the insured, usually up to age 99 or 100 subject
to policy rules.

[page 15]
Lock-in Period - In ULIPs, the lock-in period is a mandatory 5 years during which money
largely stays invested and normal withdrawals are not allowed.
25.2 - Types of Life Insurance
Life Insurance Products 15
If policyholder surrender before completing five years, the insurer first deducts
discontinuance (surrender) charges from the fund value, and the remaining amount is moved
to a separate “discontinued policy fund” where it typically earns a low, regulated interest rate
of 4% as per the policy terms. Policyholder do not get this money immediately; it is paid out
only after the original five-year lock-in ends, or to nominee if death occurs during this period.
Portfolio Flexibility - Policyholders can switch their accumulated units between different
funds (equity, debt, etc.) offered by the insurer without it being treated as a taxable
redemption. This flexibility lets investors adjust asset allocation over time based on goals
and risk profile, similar to rebalancing in mutual funds.
Various Charges - ULIPs carry multiple charges, typically including premium allocation
charges, policy administration charges, fund management charges, mortality charges for
life cover, and sometimes switching or surrender charges. Over the last 10–15 years,
IRDAI regulations have capped many of these charges and required overall cost limits, but

s for
life cover, and sometimes switching or surrender charges. Over the last 10–15 years,
IRDAI regulations have capped many of these charges and required overall cost limits, but
they still affect net returns, so a Personal Finance Professional should always evaluate
them while comparing products.
Long-Term Commitment - A ULIP is structured to deliver meaningful returns only when
held for extended durations of 10 years or more, as the impact of charges gets amortised
and the market-linked fund value has sufficient time to compound. Surrendering early not
only triggers discontinuance charges but also defeats the dual purpose of protection and
wealth creation the product is designed to serve.
Integrated Investment and Coverage - A ULIP premium is split between life insurance
cover and investment units that are allocated to chosen funds, so one product provides
both protection and growth potential. The value of the investment part moves with
holding performance, which means returns can be higher than traditional policies but are
not guaranteed.
Unit Linked Insurance Plan
A Unit-Linked Insurance Plan or a ULIP is a hybrid type of plan offered
by insurance companies that gives one the benefit of both Insurance
as well as Investments. In a ULIP, a part of the premium that one pays
is allocated towards insurance and the remaining is invested in funds

is allocated towards insurance and the remaining is invested in funds
such as stocks and bonds available within the plan.

Annuity / Pension Plan
25.2 - Types of Life Insurance
Life Insurance Products 16
Annuity or pension plans are insurance contracts that convert a lump
sum or accumulated corpus into a regular income stream, mainly for
post-retirement years. In India, life insurers and National Pension System
providers have offered annuity options for more than a decade to help
retirees manage longevity risk and maintain stable cash flows in old age.
Regular Income - Annuity plans pay a fixed or pre-agreed amount at regular intervals
(monthly, quarterly, half-yearly or yearly) after vesting date or purchase date. The vesting
date is the date from which the policyholder becomes eligible to start receiving the regular
pension or annuity payments.
Life-Long Payout - Many annuity payouts are structured as “life annuity”, where payouts
continue as long as the annuitant is alive, regardless of how long they live. This protects
against the risk of outliving one’s savings, which is a key concern in retirement planning.
Immediate and Deferred Options - There are two broad timing structures in the annuity
plans:
Immediate Annuity Annuity starts immediately after paying a lump-sum
purchase price, suited to those already at or near retirement.
Deferred Annuity
Annuity starts after deferment period. There is a gap
between paying premiums and starting the pension, called

rice, suited to those already at or near retirement.
Deferred Annuity
Annuity starts after deferment period. There is a gap
between paying premiums and starting the pension, called
the “deferment period”. During this time, the premiums or
corpus stay invested within the policy and grow, and the
actual annuity payments begin only from the vesting date.
Ideal for Generating Stable Cashflow - Annuity products are designed to provide
predictable and relatively low-risk cash flows, often backed by guaranteed rates declared
at purchase. This makes them suitable for retirees who prioritize certainty of income over
high returns.

[page 17]
Death Benefits Options - Many annuity plans in India offer different death benefit
structures, which a PFP must match to the client’s needs. Common variants include:
Life Annuity
Pays an annuity for as long as holder is alive. Stops on
annuitant’s death and then nothing is usually paid to
nominees.
Life Annuity with Return
of Purchase Price (ROP) 
Pays an annuity for life, and on annuitant’s death the
original purchase amount is returned to the nominee.
Joint Life Annuity 
Covers self and spouse both. Annuity continues to the
surviving spouse (full or reduced) after the first death,
sometimes with ROP to nominees on second death.
Children’s Policies
25.2 - Types of Life Insurance
Life Insurance Products 17
Child plans are insurance cum investment plans that help an individual
create a corpus for children's future, over a period of time (policy term).
It is suitable for young parents after covering themselves completely.
This can be given with the Premium Waiver Benefit (PWB) clause. It ensures that in the event of
the death of the premium-paying parent the policy continues normally, and the child’s future
does not suffer. In such cases, the premium is waived until the intended benefit, as per the
policy terms, reaches the child.
Benefits include:
Financial support for Child's future goals
Predetermined Cash Flow
Flexibility to choose the investment mix.

[page 18]
Group Insurance Policies
25.2 - Types of Life Insurance
Life Insurance Products 18
Group insurance policies provide insurance cover to many people
under one master contract, typically arranged by an employer, bank,
association, society or government scheme in India. Over the last 10–
15 years, group health and group term products have become popular
because they offer basic protection at lower cost and with simpler
processes than individual policies.
Unified Coverage - One policy is issued to the group organiser, and all eligible members
are covered under the same contract with common terms and conditions. This makes
administration easier and ensures a minimum level of protection for everyone in the group.
Uniform or Graded Coverage - Sum insured can be the same for all members (uniform
cover) or linked to factors like role, grade or salary (graded cover). Employers often use
graded structures to align higher cover with higher responsibility levels while still
maintaining fairness across the organisation.
Simplified Process - Group insurance usually does not require detailed medical
underwriting for each member; enrolment happens through simple data sharing and
declarations. This allows quick on-boarding of new employees or members and ensures
people with existing health conditions can still get at least basic cover.

mple data sharing and
declarations. This allows quick on-boarding of new employees or members and ensures
people with existing health conditions can still get at least basic cover.
Economical - Because risk is pooled across many people, premiums per member are
generally lower than comparable individual policies, and administrative costs are also
shared. For employers and associations, this is a cost-effective way to offer meaningful
protection benefits and improve member retention.
Flexibility - Most group policies allow members to be added or removed during the year on
a pro-rata basis as they join or leave the organisation.
Types of Group Insurance Arrangements
Employer-sponsored groups – Companies providing life or health cover to their employees
(and sometimes dependants) under one master policy.
Bank-tied groups – Banks offering group insurance to their account holders, credit-card
customers or loan borrowers.
Associations and societies – Professional bodies, clubs, co-operatives or trade associations
arranging cover for their registered members.
Government-sponsored schemes – Group covers run or supported by the government, such
as CGHS, state health schemes or other social-security health programs.

[page 19]
Keyman Insurance
Employer-Centric Coverage - Under a key man policy, the employer proposes the policy,
pays the premium and owns all rights under the contract. The employee is only the life
assured; family members do not receive the claim amount under this arrangement.
Crucial Contributor - A “key man” is typically a senior person whose skills, relationships or
decision making significantly drive revenues such as a promoter-director, star salesperson
or key technical expert. Cover is usually linked to business size and profitability, often
restricted to a multiple of recent years’ profits or salary as per insurer guidelines.
Financial Safeguard - If the key employee dies during the policy term, the company
receives the sum assured, helping it manages loss of business, repay loans, hire
replacements or stabilise cash flows. The claim is paid to the business without needing to
prove the exact monetary loss arising from the death.
25.2 - Types of Life Insurance
Life Insurance Products 19
Keyman insurance is a type of life insurance policy that covers the
business organisation for losses arising from the death of its key people.
The employer pays the premium, and if the insured person dies during
the policy term, the employer receives the death benefit.
When a business organisation feels that the absence of certain key members or people can

if the insured person dies during
the policy term, the employer receives the death benefit.
When a business organisation feels that the absence of certain key members or people can
greatly affect its performance, then it buys a keyman business insurance policy where:
The policy is proposed by the business organisation.
Premium payments are made by the business organisation.
The life of 'key' people is insured for a fixed amount.
The business organisation is the beneficiary of the policy.
Features of Keyman Insurance Policy
Tax-Effective Planning - Premiums paid by the company for a valid key man insurance
policy are generally allowed as a deductible business expense under Section 37(1) of the
Income-tax Act, 1961, subject to income-tax assessment. The death benefit is usually
taxed as business income in the hands of the company.
Summary 
For PFPs, understand these life insurance types to prioritize protection before investments,
matching client needs via suitability analysis for family income security, retirement, child
goals, or business continuity.

[page 20]

25.3
Riders
25.3 - Riders & Married Women’s Property Act
Riders & Married Women’s Property Act
Riders
Married Women’s Property Act (MWPA)
Life Insurance Products 20
A Riders in life insurance are optional add-on benefits
attached to a base life insurance policy for an extra premium.
They allow a PFP to enhance and customise a client’s
protection by covering specific risks such as accidental death,
disability, critical illness, or waiver of premium on disability, so
that a single policy addresses multiple practical risk scenarios.
Types of Riders
Accident Death and Disability Benefit Rider - This rider enhances cover if death or
disability happens specifically due to an accident, as defined in the policy.
1) Accidental Death - If the policy holder dies due to an accident, this rider pays an
additional sum assured over and above the base life cover.
2) Disability Benefit
Permanent Total Disablement (PTD) - The insured is unable to do any work ever again
due to loss of both eyes, both limbs, or similar severe impairment. Riders typically pay
100% of the rider sum assured.
Permanent Partial Disablement (PPD) - There is permanent loss or loss of use of a
listed body part (one eye, one limb, fingers, etc.), but the person can still do some
work. The payout is a percentage of rider sum assured “as per rules”, such as 10%–

of use of a
listed body part (one eye, one limb, fingers, etc.), but the person can still do some
work. The payout is a percentage of rider sum assured “as per rules”, such as 10%–
75% of sum assured, depending on which part is affected.
Many ADDB riders also include automatic waiver of future premiums on the base
policy and remaining riders on occurrence of defined permanent disability, so that the
life cover continues even when the client cannot pay premiums.

[page 21]
Critical Illness Rider - A critical illness rider provides a lump-sum benefit on first diagnosis
of specified major illnesses. It is not based on hospital bills but on meeting the policy
definition.
Income Benefit Rider due to Disability - This rider converts the financial impact of
disability into a predictable regular income stream for the family. It is often attached along
with a disability rider.
Waiver of Premium Rider (WOP) - If this is not available as a benefit under ADDB rider,
such a benefit may also be added as a WOP rider. On total and permanent disablement
due to an accident, all future premiums both under the basic policy and the rider/s will be
waived till the end of the term of the rider or death of the assured life, if earlier.
Married Women’s Property Act (MWPA)
Life Insurance Products 21
On diagnosis of a covered illness (for example, certain types of cancer, heart attack of
specified severity, stroke, major organ transplant), and after any required survival
period, the rider pays a pre-agreed amount.
This rider helps the insured person manage medical expenses or compensate for lost
income due to the illness.
Once the pay-out is made, the rider terminates while the life cover under the base
plan and other riders continues (if any).
If the policy holder suffers with disability due to accident and/or illness-related,

rider terminates while the life cover under the base
plan and other riders continues (if any).
If the policy holder suffers with disability due to accident and/or illness-related,
depending on product terms, the insurer pays a fixed monthly income for a pre-
decided number of months, which helps replace their lost earnings.
If the policyholder becomes disabled, they receive a fixed monthly income for a pre-
decided number of months, which helps replace their lost earnings.
This ensures that the policyholder’s family can maintain the same lifestyle even when
the insured person cannot work due to disability.
The Married Women’s Property Act, 1874 (MWPA) can be
used with a life insurance policy to lock in the policy proceeds
only for the wife and/or children of the life assured. Once
endorsed under MWPA at proposal stage, the policy legally
becomes a small trust for these beneficiaries and stays
outside the policyholder’s estate.
25.3 - Riders & Married Women’s Property Act

[page 22]
MWP Act Purpose - Protects a married woman’s financial rights by ensuring that the sum
assured from a life policy is treated as her (and/or children’s) separate property, not as part
of the husband’s estate.
Protection from Creditors - Proceeds of a policy endorsed under MWPA cannot be
claimed by business creditors, lenders or any other third party; they are payable only to the
named beneficiaries.
Life Insurance Products 22
In case of death of the life assured, the benefit passes directly and exclusively to
wife/children, even if there are family disputes, HUF issues or competing claims on
other assets.
A married woman can also use MWPA to secure a policy on her own life exclusively for
her children, ensuring that the benefit does not get diverted in wider family disputes
or creditor actions.
Nomination Limitation - Only the wife, or children, or wife together with children can be
set as beneficiaries, and these names and their shares must be decided at inception and
cannot be changed later.
Protection for Family
MWPA Endorsement must be opted at the start of the policy; it is generally not
available later.
Key Conditions
The policy effectively acts as a statutory trust, so a separate trust deed is not required.
Summary 
For a Personal Finance Professional (PFP), riders help enhance and customise life insurance

ffectively acts as a statutory trust, so a separate trust deed is not required.
Summary 
For a Personal Finance Professional (PFP), riders help enhance and customise life insurance
policies to address multiple risk scenarios such as death, disability, and critical illness within a
single plan. They enable better client protection by converting uncertainties into structured
financial support like lump sum or income replacement.
Additionally, understanding MWPA provisions allows PFPs to safeguard policy proceeds
exclusively for the client’s spouse and children, ensuring protection from creditors and family
disputes. Together, riders and MWPA strengthen comprehensive risk planning and secure
client outcomes.

Eligibility
For individual clients, premiums paid for life insurance qualify for deduction under Section
80C within the overall limit of ₹1.5 lakh per financial year.
In this topic, we will cover the tax benefits on life insurance premiums at the time of payment
and at the time of receiving policy benefits.
A resident individual or HUF can claim deduction on life insurance premiums paid for self,
spouse and children, but not for parents, in-laws or siblings, which PFPs must explain
clearly to clients.
Conditions
If the policy is surrendered within two years (for regular policies) or before five years in
case of ULIPs, earlier 80C deductions can be reversed and added back to income in the
year of surrender.

Life Insurance Products 24
1st Condition - For traditional and term policies with maturity value, proceeds are tax-free
if the annual premium has never exceeded 10% of the sum assured for policies issued on

lakh in any year.
Taxation of life insurance claims and proceeds is mainly governed by Section 10(10D) of the
Income-tax Act.
1) Death Claims - Any amount received by nominees on the death of the life assured (sum

irrespective of premium amount, policy issue date, or number of policies.
2) Maturity Proceeds

tax-free under Section 10(10D) only if the aggregate annual premium of all such
policies does not exceed ₹2.5 lakh in any year during the policy term.

 Terminal Illness
• In the event the Life Assured is diagnosed with a Terminal Illness during the Policy Term, for an In-force 
 policy, Death Beneﬁt will be payable to the Claimant. 
• Terminal Illness Beneﬁt only accelerates the Death Beneﬁt payable under the Policy and is not an 
 additional beneﬁt. 
• On payment of this beneﬁt, the Policy will terminate and all rights, beneﬁts and interests under the policy 
 will stand extinguished.
• A Life Assured shall be regarded as Terminally Ill only if that Life Assured is diagnosed as suffering from 
 a condition which, in the opinion of two independent Medical Practitioners specializing in treatment of 
 such illness, is highly likely to lead to death within 6 months. The Terminal Illness must be diagnosed and 
 conﬁrmed by Medical Practitioners registered with the Indian Medical Association and approved by the 
 Company. The Company reserves the right for an independent assessment.
• Terminal Illness Beneﬁt will not be available in case policy is sourced through POS personnel.

26.1
Key Parameters while Choosing Health Insurance
Right Coverage Amount - The sum insured should reflect the client's actual healthcare
exposure — their city of residence, age, family size, and existing health conditions all play
a role. A ₹5 lakh cover may have been adequate a decade ago, but rising hospitalisation
costs in cities mean most families today need a minimum of ₹10–25 lakh coverage.

4
Health insurance helps a family stay financially secure during medical
emergencies by covering hospital and treatment bills that could
otherwise disturb long-term financial goals. Insurers in India design
health plans with a range of sum insured options, flexible features and
relatively affordable premiums with lifetime renewability for most people.
In addition, premiums paid for eligible health insurance policies qualify for tax deductions
(subject to old tax regime) under Section 80D of the Income-tax Act, which encourages families
to protect their health while also reducing taxable income, subject to prescribed limits and
conditions.

to protect their health while also reducing taxable income, subject to prescribed limits and
conditions.
Premium Charges - Annual premium is usually paid in advance for health insurance, and it
depends on age, sum insured, family size and medical history. Many insurers are now
providing different premium payment modes such as monthly, quarterly and half-yearly, in
addition to annual mode.
General Insurance Products

[page 5]
Pre & Post Hospitalization Cost - Most health policies cover diagnostic tests, consultations
and medicines for a fixed number of days before admission and after discharge, such as 90
days pre and 180 days post.
26.1 - Health Insurance Policy
5
Example: Assume a client buys health insurance with a base sum insured of ₹5 lakh and
20% NCB per claim-free year. After 1 year without any claim, the effective sum insured
becomes ₹6 lakh (₹5 lakh base + ₹1 lakh cumulative bonus).
Day Care Procedures - These are treatments or surgeries requiring less than 24 hours of
hospitalization due to advanced medical technology. The number and type of listed day
care procedures vary across insurers, so PFPs must review this list carefully for common
procedures like cataract, dialysis and chemotherapy.
Domiciliary Treatment - Domiciliary hospitalization means hospital-like treatment taken at
home when the patient cannot be moved or a bed is unavailable. Coverage is typically
subject to specific illnesses, limits and exclusions.
Moratorium Period - As per IRDAI, once a policy completes 5 continuous years of coverage
(including portability or migration), the insurer cannot contest the policy or deny claims for
non-disclosure or misrepresentation, except in proven fraud cases. The 5-year moratorium
applies separately to any later increase in sum insured, from the date of enhancement.

non-disclosure or misrepresentation, except in proven fraud cases. The 5-year moratorium
applies separately to any later increase in sum insured, from the date of enhancement.
Restoration Benefit - Restoration benefit automatically reinstates the sum insured (partly
or fully) after it is exhausted by claims, allowing further claims in the same policy year.
PFPs must read policy conditions such as activation only after full exhaustion, use for
unrelated illnesses, and whether restoration works once or multiple times in a year.
No Claim Bonus (NCB) – NCB in health insurance is a reward for a claim-free policy year,
usually given at renewal. Most insurers increase the sum insured by a fixed percentage
(called cumulative bonus) every year without a claim, up to a maximum limit; some may
instead or additionally offer a discount on the renewal premium. If there is a claim in a later
year, the accumulated NCB typically reduces as per the policy terms but the base sum
insured remains protected.
Pre-Existing Diseases (PED) - PEDs are illnesses that existed before policy purchased and
were disclosed in the proposal form, and they are covered only after a defined waiting
period, often 2 to 3 years. If a policyholder fails to disclose a pre-existing condition, the
insurer has the legal right to repudiate the claim and cancel the policy

Room Rent / ICU Charges - Policies may cap room rent as a percentage of sum insured or
a fixed amount, or may allow any room without a cap. Room eligibility directly influences
all linked costs like nursing, doctor fees and ICU charges, so exceeding the eligible
category can lead to proportionate claim reduction.
General Insurance Products

Organ Donor Expenses - Standard policies usually cover medical expenses of the organ
recipient (insured person), while organ donor related costs are covered only if mentioned
in the policy.
Miscellaneous Benefits
26.1 - Health Insurance Policy
6
These days, with the increasing number of organ transplant surgeries in India, many
insurance providers have now introduced health insurance plans, which can provide cover
for the expenses incurred by both donor and recipient in organ transplantation.
Emergency Road/Air ambulance - Most health policies cover road
ambulance expenses up to a fixed limit or percentage of sum insured
when hospitalization is admissible; some higher-end plans also cover
air ambulance for life-threatening emergencies.
Health check-up / Preventive check-up - Many insurers provide
periodic health or preventive check-ups after a claim-free period or
from day one, often as part of the policy rather than at extra cost.
Network Hospitals - Network hospitals are those with a tie-up for
cashless treatment; the insurer settles eligible bills directly with the
hospital. PFPs should help clients check whether good quality
hospitals near their home or workplace are on the network list,
rather than only counting the total number of hospitals.
Cashless Claim Settlement - Cashless settlement allows insured persons

ear their home or workplace are on the network list,

Cashless Claim Settlement - Cashless settlement allows insured persons
to get admitted in a network hospital without paying the main hospital
bill; they show their policy e-card or policy number and pay only
non-covered expenses.
Portability - Portability allows policyholders in India to switch
between insurers without losing prior accrued benefits like no-claim
bonuses or waiting periods served. This feature ensures seamless
continuity of coverage, provided the new policy is purchased within
45 days before the existing policy expires.
Non-Medical Expenses Coverage - Hospitalisation bills routinely include consumables —
gloves, syringes, PPE kits, bandages — that standard health policies exclude and the
patient must pay out of pocket. Policies that cover non-medical expenses absorb these
costs, reducing the gap between what the insurer pays and what the hospital bills.

Meaning
Deductible is the fixed amount of hospital/medical expenses that the policyholder must bear
before the insurer starts paying under top-up or super top-up policy. It shifts a portion of risk
to the client and keeps premiums lower, especially in top-up and super top-up plans.
Number of Claims Considered
Super top-up policy counts the cumulative eligible hospital expenses in a policy year. Once
total of approved bills crosses the deductible limit, the super top-up starts paying for
further expenses in that year, even if this happens over several small claims.
Regular top-up policy, in contrast, usually works claim-wise: it pays only when a single
hospitalization bill exceeds the deductible limit, so multiple small claims that individually
stay below the deductible may not be covered.

injuries; most PA policies pay 100% of the sum insured in such cases.

There are three commonly used valuation approaches in India for home building and contents:
1.Market Value (depreciated cost basis)

1) Market Value (Depreciated Cost Basis)

3.Agreed Value Basis
1) Market Value (Depreciated Cost Basis)
Market value means the new replacement or reconstruction cost minus depreciation for age
and wear-and-tear.
At claim time, the insurer pays the depreciated value of the property, so the client may have
to add their own funds to fully rebuild or replace the property.
2) Reinstatement Value (Reconstruction Cost Basis)
Reinstatement value means the cost of reconstructing or replacing the property with a
similar new one at current prices, without deducting depreciation, subject to the sum
insured.
The insured must actually rebuild/repair within a specified time and as per policy
conditions; insurers often pay in stages against proof of reconstruction.
General Insurance Products

[page 24]
26.5 - Home Insurance Policy
24
3) Agreed Value Basis
Under agreed value, the insurer and policyholder mutually fix a value for the building or
contents at proposal stage, and this becomes the reference amount for settling a total-loss
claim.
The claim is normally paid on this pre-agreed value (subject to policy terms), and is not
automatically adjusted for future depreciation or market price changes, giving greater
certainty to the client.
Let’s understand with this example,
Suppose a house has a current reconstruction cost of ₹50 lakhs.
On a market value basis, the insurer first applies depreciation for age and wear-and-tear
say 30% so the market value becomes ₹35 lakhs. If there is a total loss, the claim is settled
around ₹35 lakhs and the owner must arrange the remaining ₹15 lakhs to rebuild a similar
house.
On a reinstatement value basis, the sum insured is kept at the full ₹50 lakhs, and if the
owner actually reconstructs the house as per policy conditions, the insurer reimburses the
reasonable reconstruction cost up to ₹50 lakhs without deducting depreciation.
Under an agreed value basis, the insurer and owner pre-fix a value say ₹45 lakhs as the
insured value; if a total loss occurs and the claim is admitted, the insurer pays ₹45 lakhs
irrespective of later depreciation or actual reconstruction cost, and the owner is free to

sured value; if a total loss occurs and the claim is admitted, the insurer pays ₹45 lakhs
irrespective of later depreciation or actual reconstruction cost, and the owner is free to
either rebuild or purchase a different property using this agreed amount.
For PFPs, there is no single best option; suitability depends on the client’s property type and
objectives.
For standalone houses where reconstruction is practical and desired, reinstatement value
usually offers the most appropriate protection, as it aims to restore the same house without
depreciation.
For older properties where clients accept some gap in funding, market value can be a
lower-premium choice. 
For single-flat owners in multi-storey buildings, agreed value is often more practical, as it
provides a clear lump sum to buy or shift to another home even if society-wide
reconstruction is delayed.

I.1.1 The International Monetary Fund (IMF), in its
April 2025 issue of World Economic Outlook Update,
reported a slowdown in global growth as downside
risks intensified amid rising policy uncertainty and
structural shifts in the global trade environment.
Following a series of unprecedented events in recent
years—including the pandemic, geopolitical conflicts,
and inflation surges—the global economy showed
signs of stabilization in 2024, with inflation gradually
declining and labour markets returning to pre-
pandemic levels. Under the reference forecast, global
headline inflation was expected to decline to 4.3
percent in 2025 and to 3.6 percent in 2026. Growth
remains modest and projections for global output
have been revised downward from the January 2025
update. Growth was projected at 2.8 percent in 2025
and 3.0 percent in 2026, marking a cumulative
downgrade of 0.8 percentage points from earlier
forecasts and remaining well below the 2000–2019
historical average of 3.7 percent. This reflects
heightened downside risks, including the potential
escalation of trade tensions and increased trade
policy uncertainty.

I.2 Appraisal of Insurance Market
I.2.1 Appraisal of Global Insurance Market
I.2.1.1 The Swiss Re Sigma Report (No. 2/2025)
highlights that after a strong performance in 2024,
premium growth in the world’s insurance industry is
slowing on both the non-life and life sides, impacted
by global economic slowdown and the unstable policy
environment. According to the Swiss Re estimates
total premiums (life and non-life) to grow at 2 per
cent in real terms in 2025 compared to 5.2 per cent
in 2024, with a marginal pick-up to 2.3 per cent in
2026. Heightened geopolitical shifts and rising de-
globalisation rhetoric pose additional risks to the re/
insurance sector that relies on global risk pooling and
international capital movements. Such fragmentation
would impede risk diversification, increases cost of
insurance and curtail the contribution of the industry
to narrowing existing protection gaps.

1. The IRDAI, in order to protect the interest of the policyholders and to ensure that the premiums are
collected upon the successful underwriting of proposal, has mandated through its Master Circular on
Protection of Policyholders Interests, 2024, that insurers can collect premiums only after the proposal
submitted by the prospect has been accepted except in cases of policies issued basis declaration of
good health where risk cover commences immediately on receipt of premium.
2. In order to provide operational ease in meeting with this requirement, the Authority has allowed the
facility of one-time mandate for holding the amounts towards premium payment.
3. Under this facility called the “Bima Applications Supported by Blocked Amount (Bima - ASBA)” transfer
of money from the prospect to the insurer happens only when insurance policy is issued. In this facility,
insurers can offer one-time mandate for blocking certain amount through Unified Payment Interface
(UPI) in the bank account of the concerned prospect. Amount towards insurance premium will be debited
only after the insurer decides to accept the proposal. In case the insurer does not accept the proposal,
the amount shall be unblocked and shall be released and shall be available at the disposal of the
prospect.

I.6.2 Maintenance of Solvency Margins of
Insurers
I.6.2.1 Every insurer and reinsurer shall at all times
maintain solvency margin higher than the control level
of solvency, which currently is 150 per cent of
Required Solvency Margin, i.e. to ensure that the
Available Solvency Margin is at least 150 per cent of
Required Solvency Margin at all times. The Required
Solvency Margin shall not be less than fifty per cent
of the amount of minimum capital as stated under
Section 6 of the Insurance Act, 1938 whereas the
Available Solvency Margin is the excess of value of
assets over the amount of liabilities. The IRDAI
(Actuarial, Finance and Investment Functions of
Insurers) Regulations, 2024 describe in detail the

India underwent a comprehensive Financial Sector Assessment Program (FSAP) in 2024, jointly conducted by the

assets over the amount of liabilities. The IRDAI

Ways of Buying Home Insurance
1) Market Value (Depreciated Cost Basis)
Replacement/reconstruction cost after deducting depreciation for age and wear.
Insurer pays only the depreciated amount; client bears the gap to fully rebuild.
2) Reinstatement Value (Reconstruction Cost Basis)
Full current-price reconstruction cost, with no depreciation deducted, up to the sum insured.
Insured must actually rebuild within policy timelines; payment is released in stages against proof.
3) Agreed Value Basis
Insurer and policyholder fix a mutually agreed value at policy inception for total-loss settlement.
Claim is paid at that pre-agreed amount, unaffected by future depreciation or market changes.

Mutual Fund - Basics
How a Mutual Fund Works?

Mutual Funds - Categories & Risks 3
Meaning
A mutual fund is a collective investment vehicle that collects & pools money from a number of
investors and invests the same in equities, bonds, government securities, money market
instruments.
Mutual Funds in India are established in the form of a Trust under Indian Trust Act, 1882, in
accordance with SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996. The fees and expenses charged by the
mutual funds to manage a scheme are regulated and are subject to the limits specified by SEBI.
Source - AMFI (Association of Mutual Funds in India)
How a Mutual Fund Works?

[page 4]
Structure of Mutual Fund in India
27.1 - Mutual Fund - Basics
Mutual Funds - Categories & Risks 4
In a mutual fund, many investors pool their money with a fund house (also called an Asset
Management Company), which then appoints a professional fund manager to handle the
investments. The fund manager invests this pooled money in various securities such as shares,
bonds or gold, as per the scheme’s stated objective. As these investments gain or lose value, the
profit or loss is reflected in the mutual fund’s portfolio and the resulting returns are passed back
to investors in proportion to the units they hold.
In India, the mutual fund structure involves several key entities, each with a clearly defined role
under SEBI (Mutual Fund) Regulations, 1996. Their combined objective is to protect investors’
interests and ensure that money is managed in a transparent and professional manner.
Source - AMFI
There are three core entities in the mutual fund structure in India,
The Sponsor (who creates a Mutual Fund)
The Trustees
The Asset Management Company (AMC)
Together, they create, oversee and manage mutual fund schemes within the regulatory framework
laid down by SEBI.
Sponsor - The sponsor is the promoter who takes the initiative to set up the mutual fund
and must meet SEBI’s eligibility criteria on financial strength, track record and integrity.

ponsor - The sponsor is the promoter who takes the initiative to set up the mutual fund
and must meet SEBI’s eligibility criteria on financial strength, track record and integrity.
The sponsor approaches SEBI for approval, and after receiving approval, constitutes a
public trust under the Indian Trusts Act, 1882 and promotes an AMC to manage
investments.

[page 5]
27.1 - Mutual Fund - Basics
Mutual Funds - Categories & Risks 5
Trustees - Trustees form the second layer and act as protectors of unit holders’ interests,
either as a Trustee Company or a Board of Trustees. They hold the mutual fund’s property
in trust for investors, supervise the AMC and ensure that all activities comply with SEBI
(Mutual Fund) Regulations and the trust deed.
Asset Management Companies - The AMC is the investment manager to the trust and is
incorporated under the Companies Act in India. For a regulated fee, the AMC designs
schemes, manages portfolios, handles operations and engages with intermediaries such as
brokers, custodians, bankers and service providers, while adhering to SEBI rules.
Custodian - A custodian is responsible for the safekeeping of the securities of the mutual
fund. They manage the investment account of the mutual fund, ensure the delivery and
transfer of the securities. They also collect and track the dividends & interests received on
the mutual fund investment.
Registrar and Transfer Agents (RTAs) - These are the entities who provide services to
mutual funds. RTAs are more like the operational arm of Mutual Funds. 
They process applications, maintain investor records, issue account statements, update
changes in details and support AMCs with standardized, cost-efficient operations across
schemes.

y process applications, maintain investor records, issue account statements, update
changes in details and support AMCs with standardized, cost-efficient operations across
schemes.
CAMS & Kfintech are some of the well-known RTAs in India.
Fund Accountants - Fund accountants calculate the value of the fund’s assets and make
sure everything adds up correctly. They help figure out what each unit is worth and make
sure accounts are managed properly.
Bankers - Bankers help with transactions, payments, and moving money in and out of the
fund. They ensure that money is transferred quickly and safely whenever investors invest
or withdraw.
Agents/ Distributors - Agents and distributors are people or organizations who help
investors learn about mutual funds and make investments. They act as a bridge between
the investors and the mutual fund companies. In addition, they handle paperwork and
make the whole experience easier and faster for investors. Agents earn a commission for
these services from AMC.
Investors - Investors are the ultimate owners who contribute money to the mutual fund
and receive units in return. They benefit from professional management, diversification
and regulatory oversight, with their interests safeguarded by trustees and supported by all
the other entities in the mutual fund ecosystem.
