PMS – Evaluation
3
Portfolio Management Services (PMS) are regulated investment products where a professional
portfolio manager handles a customised basket of securities for an individual client, typically a
high-net-worth investor. 
Unlike pooled vehicles such as mutual funds, each PMS account is held and reported separately
in the client’s name, and buy–sell decisions are taken at the portfolio level in line with an
agreed mandate, risk profile and investment philosophy.
SEBI Regulation – PMS Industry in India is regulated by SEBI, with a minimum investment
corpus of Rs.50 lakh for eligibility.
Client Base – PMS caters to HNIs, UHNIs, NRIs & institutions seeking professional
portfolio management services.
Tailored Portfolios – PMS crafts personalized portfolios with diverse securities based on
client goals and risk tolerance.
Fee Model / Profit Sharing – PMS charge a percentage of AUM &/or Profit sharing as a fee
for professional management services.
Diverse Strategies – PMS employs varied investment strategies (value, growth, income,
quantitative) and provides regular performance updates for client transparency.

PMS, AIF & SIF

[page 4]
Types of PMS
4
PMS can be categorized into several types based on the level of control and strategy
implementation:
1) Discretionary Portfolio Management
In Discretionary Portfolio Management, investors delegate the decision-making authority
to the fund manager.
This hands-off approach allows the fund manager to make investment decisions on behalf
of the investor, considering their objectives and risk tolerance.
The portfolio manager has complete control of the investment portfolio.
The investor benefits from professional expertise and timely adjustments to the portfolio in
response to market dynamics.
2) Non-Discretionary Portfolio Management
Non-Discretionary Portfolio Management involves a collaborative approach between the
investor and the fund manager.
While the fund manager provides recommendations and insights, the final investment
decisions rest with the investor.
The manager advises, but the investor is responsible for the decisions. More of an advisory
role.
This type of service is ideal for investors who want to stay informed and involved in the
decision-making process.
3) Advisory Portfolio Management

Advantages
PMS holds a focused set of stocks reflecting the manager's strongest convictions, unlike a

The manager can freely adjust holdings and sector exposure without the constraints an

Stocks are held in the investor's own demat account, giving full legal ownership rather

Alternative Investment Fund (AIF) is a privately pooled investment vehicle that invests in
alternative asset classes such as private equity, venture capital, hedge funds, real estate,
commodities, and derivatives. Generally, HNIs (High net worth individuals) and institutions
invest in the AIFs as the investment amount is substantially higher.
AIFs are regulated by the SEBI (Securities and Exchange Board of India). As per the SEBI
(Alternative Investment Funds) Regulations, 2012, an AIF can be set up as a trust, a company, a
limited liability partnership, or a corporate body. However, many of the AIFs that have been
registered with SEBI are in the form of trusts.
High Minimum Investment - AIFs usually require at least ₹1 crore per investor, so target
investors are high-net-worth individuals and institutions.
Hybrid Approach - AIFs combine mutual-fund-like pooling with PMS-like flexibility in
portfolio construction and strategy design.
Specialised Investment Strategies - AIFs can invest in hedge funds, private equity, venture
capital, real estate, REITs and other alternative assets, ensuring portfolio diversification.

alised Investment Strategies - AIFs can invest in hedge funds, private equity, venture
capital, real estate, REITs and other alternative assets, ensuring portfolio diversification.
Category Structure - SEBI divides AIFs into three categories (Category I, II and III), each
with distinct mandates, risk profiles and regulatory treatment.

33.2 - AIF (Alternative Investment Fund)

[page 14]
14
SEBI has categorized Alternative Investment Funds into 3 categories:
Investment in Equity and Debt Securities. They are typically closed-ended funds aiming for
long-term capital appreciation.
Venture Capital Fund (VCF) - New-age entrepreneurial firms that require large financing
during their initial days can approach VCF. VCF can help them in overcoming the financial
crunch. These funds invest in start-ups with high growth prospects. HNIs investing in VCFs
adopt a high-risk, high-return strategy while allocating their resources.
Private Equity (PE) Funds - A private equity fund invests in unlisted private companies. It is
difficult for unlisted companies to raise funds by issuing equity and debt instruments.
Usually, these funds come with a lock-in period which ranges from 4 to 7 years. 
Unlisted / Private Debt Funds - This fund primarily invests in debt securities of unlisted
companies. Usually, such companies follow good corporate governance models and have
high growth potential. They have a low credit rating, which makes them a risky option for
conservative investors. As per SEBI guidelines, money accumulated by debt funds cannot
be used to give loans.
Fund of Funds - Such funds invest in other Alternative Investment Funds. They do not
have their investment portfolio but focus on investing in different AIFs.
Category 1 AIFs

have their investment portfolio but focus on investing in different AIFs.
Category 1 AIFs
These funds invest in SMEs, start-ups, and new economically viable businesses with high
growth potential.
Angel Funds - These invest in budding start-ups and are called angel investors. They bring
early business management experience with them. These funds invest in those start-ups
that do not receive funding from VCF. The minimum investment by each angel investor is
Rs 25 lakh.
Infrastructure Fund - This fund invests in infrastructure companies, i.e., those involved in
railway construction, port construction, etc. Investors who are bullish on infrastructure
development invest their money in these funds. 
Social Venture Funds - Funds investing in a socially responsible business are social venture
funds. They are a kind of philanthropic investment but have a scope of generating decent
returns for investors. 
Category 2 AIFs
33.2 - AIF (Alternative Investment Fund)
PMS, AIF & SIF

[page 15]
15
This category uses complex, often market-linked strategies and can employ leverage and
derivatives. They are usually suited only for sophisticated investors comfortable with higher
risk and active trading styles.
Real Estate Fund - Invest in property projects or property-backed securities, such as
residential or commercial developments, warehousing, or income-yielding assets. They
may fund developers through equity or structured debt, with returns coming from project
completion, leasing, sale of units or re-rating of completed assets.
Private Investment in Public Equity Fund (PIPE) - A PIPE invests in shares of publicly
traded companies. They acquire shares at a discounted price. Investment through PIPE is
more convenient than going for a secondary issue owing to less paperwork and
administration.
Hedge Funds - Hedge funds pool money from accredited investors and institutions. These
funds invest in both domestic and international debt and equity markets. They may follow
styles such as long-short equity, event-driven, relative-value or macro, and their
benchmark is often absolute return or low correlation to equity indices rather than simple
outperformance of an index. They adopt an aggressive investment strategy to generate
returns for investors.
Commodity Funds - Invest in commodities such as metals, energy or agricultural products,

f an index. They adopt an aggressive investment strategy to generate
returns for investors.
Commodity Funds - Invest in commodities such as metals, energy or agricultural products,
primarily through exchange-traded derivatives or commodity-linked securities, rather than
physically holding the commodities. For portfolios, they can offer diversification against
traditional equity and debt, but returns are highly sensitive to global supply-demand
dynamics, currency moves, and regulation.
Category 3 AIFs
Listed Debt Funds - Focus on actively trading listed bonds, debentures and money-market
instruments, often using derivatives such as interest-rate futures or credit derivatives
where permitted. Unlike passive hold-to-maturity bond strategies, these funds try to profit
from changes in interest rates, credit spreads and liquidity, and may use leverage to
enhance returns.
33.2 - AIF (Alternative Investment Fund)
PMS, AIF & SIF

[page 16]
16
Diversification - AIFs offer investors the opportunity to diversify their portfolios beyond
traditional assets. By investing in alternative asset classes, investors can reduce their
exposure to market volatility and potentially improve risk-adjusted returns.
Potential for Higher Returns - Alternative investments often have the potential to generate
higher returns compared to traditional investments. For example, private equity and
venture capital funds can deliver substantial gains if successful investments are made.
Professional & Specialized Management - AIFs are run by experienced fund managers with
deep sector or strategy-specific expertise. This specialization allows for more informed
decision-making in complex asset classes.
Advantages
High Entry Barrier - Only high-net-worth individuals and institutions can meet this
investment threshold. This makes AIFs inaccessible to retail or smaller investors.
AIF Advantages & Disadvantages
Flexibility in Strategies - Fund managers can use advanced techniques like short-selling,
PIPE deals, and derivatives that mutual funds cannot. This flexibility allows AIFs to
potentially generate returns in both rising and falling markets.
Disadvantages
Lock-in Period for Cat I & II - For Cat I & II, Investor capital remains committed for a lock-in

s to
potentially generate returns in both rising and falling markets.
Disadvantages
Lock-in Period for Cat I & II - For Cat I & II, Investor capital remains committed for a lock-in
period of 3 to 10 years or an extended period with no early exit option. This requires
investors to be certain about their liquidity needs before committing.
Higher Risk - Investments in unlisted securities and leveraged derivative positions carry
greater volatility and downside risk. This requires investors to have a higher risk tolerance
than typical mutual fund investors.
33.2 - AIF (Alternative Investment Fund)
PMS, AIF & SIF
Pass-through Taxation in Cat I & II - Gains are taxed directly in the hands of investors
rather than at the fund level for these categories. This avoids double taxation and keeps
the tax treatment aligned with the nature of the underlying gains.
Lock-in Period for Cat III - Some Category III AIFs are closed-end and restrict redemption
to a fixed maturity date rather than allowing anytime exit. This adds a further liquidity
constraint on top of the fund's inherent complexity.

[page 17]
Complex Taxation in Cat III - Unlike Cat I & II, Category III AIFs are taxed at the fund level,
often at the maximum marginal rate. This makes post-tax return calculations less
straightforward for investors.
Liquidity Risk - Many AIFs have lock-in periods, meaning investor capital is committed for
a specific duration. It can be a challenge if investor need liquidity.
Complexity Risk - Understanding AIF structures and risks can be challenging, especially for
investors with less financial investment experience.

18
The Specialized Investment Fund (SIF) is a new category of investment product introduced by
SEBI to bridge the gap between Mutual Funds (MFs) and Portfolio Management Services
(PMS). SIFs aim to provide a middle ground, offering portfolio flexibility while ensuring
regulatory compliance and investor protection.
Well-Positioned to Serve Targeted Investment Needs
PMS, AIF & SIF

[page 19]
Features of SIF
Minimum Investment - SIFs require a ₹10 lakh minimum per investor, applied across all SIF
strategies of a single AMC on a PAN basis. This higher threshold positions SIF between
mutual funds and PMS, targeting investors who want more sophisticated strategies
without the ₹50 lakh PMS entry barrier.
Short-Selling Allowed up to 25% - Fund managers can take unhedged short positions using
derivatives, up to 25% of the fund's net assets. This allows SIFs to potentially generate
returns even in falling markets, a capability traditional mutual funds don't have.
Liquidity Varies by Strategy - Redemption frequency differs by strategy type. Daily for
Equity, weekly for Debt, and twice a week for Hybrid. This tiered liquidity structure
reflects the relative complexity and risk of each underlying strategy category.
SEBI Regulated but Flexible - SIFs operate under SEBI's Mutual Fund Regulations, giving
investors the regulatory oversight and tax efficiency associated with mutual funds. At the
same time, they permit PMS-like tools such as short-selling and derivatives, offering a
genuine middle ground between the two product types.

What is SIF?
Specialised Investment Fund (SIF) is a new category of investment product introduced by SEBI to bridge the gap between Mutual Funds (MFs) and Portfolio Management Services (PMS). SIFs aim to provide a middle ground, offering portfolio flexibility while ensuring regulatory compliance and investor protection.

Hybrid Long-Short Fund - Maintains a balanced investment in both equity and debt instruments

Residential Real Estate
Residential Types
Apartments - Apartments are individual housing units within a larger building or complex.
They are common in cities where land is limited and shared amenities reduce individual
costs. They suit working professionals and small families who prefer convenience and
easier maintenance.
Independent Houses - Independent houses are standalone homes built on separate plots.
They offer more privacy, open space and control over home design and modifications.
However, the owner is fully responsible for security, repairs and upkeep, which can be
time-consuming and costly.
Villas - Villas are premium independent homes, usually inside gated communities. They offer
larger built-up areas, private gardens & facilities like clubhouses or pools. These properties
are typically chosen by higher-income households seeking more space & exclusivity.
Residential real estate refers to land and buildings used mainly for
living purposes, such as houses and apartments. It is different from
commercial real estate, which is meant for business use like offices
or shops. Residential properties can still generate income when

as houses and apartments. It is different from
commercial real estate, which is meant for business use like offices
or shops. Residential properties can still generate income when
rented, or create wealth when sold at a higher price. For most
Indian families, it is often the first and largest long-term asset.

[page 4]
34.1 - Investment Options in Real Estate
Real Estate & Gold 4
Purpose
Capital Appreciation
Flats - Flats in India generally mean apartment-style homes in multi-storey buildings. They
come in standard sizes like 1BHK to 4BHK and are often designed to be compact and
relatively affordable. Many middle-income families prefer flats in organised projects that
provide basic amenities and community living.
Rental Income
Stability and Security
Emotional Satisfaction
Market Size
The residential real estate market in India has expanded with rising incomes and urbanisation.
Demand exists across affordable, mid-income and luxury segments, with larger homes gaining
interest after the pandemic. Many buyers now look for better layouts, open spaces and
community facilities rather than just a basic shelter.
Luxury housing has also become more visible in major cities and fast-growing suburbs.
Higher-income households show willingness to pay for branded developments, gated security
and lifestyle amenities. For Personal Finance Professionals (PFPs), this means clients may
allocate a bigger share of savings to high-value homes.
Net-worth
In planning, a self-occupied home is usually treated differently from investment assets.
Although its market value may be high, it does not generate regular income and is not easily

n planning, a self-occupied home is usually treated differently from investment assets.
Although its market value may be high, it does not generate regular income and is not easily
sold without affecting the family’s lifestyle. Hence, many PFPs keep it outside the “investable”
portfolio while still noting its value.
By separating emotional assets like the main home from productive assets, PFPs get a clearer
view of a client’s financial strength. This approach helps design realistic strategies for
retirement, child’s education and other financial goals.

[page 5]
Commercial Real Estate
Office Spaces - Office buildings house businesses such as IT companies, banks, and
professional firms. They are usually located in business districts with good connectivity
and infrastructure. Long-term leases with corporate tenants can provide relatively stable
rental income.
Retail Shops and Malls - Retail spaces include high-street shops, showrooms and shopping
malls. Their success depends on visibility, footfall and tenant mix. Rental income may vary
with consumer demand and overall economic conditions.
Industrial Buildings and Warehouses - These properties are used for manufacturing, storage
and logistics. Demand has grown with e-commerce, organised retail and supply chain
expansion. Locations near highways, ports and transport hubs are preferred.
34.1 - Investment Options in Real Estate
Real Estate & Gold 5
Commercial Real Estate (CRE) refers to properties used mainly
for business activities rather than for living. These properties
are leased or sold to tenants who run offices, shops,
warehouses, hotels or other commercial operations. The main
objective is to generate income through rent and long-term
value growth. For many Indian investors, CRE is a way to earn
higher income compared with typical residential rentals.
Types of CRE Investments
Hospitality, Mixed-use and Medical Buildings - Hotels, serviced apartments and resorts fall

o earn
higher income compared with typical residential rentals.
Types of CRE Investments
Hospitality, Mixed-use and Medical Buildings - Hotels, serviced apartments and resorts fall
under hospitality. Mixed-use projects combine offices, retail and residences in one complex.
Medical buildings include clinics and hospitals that cater to healthcare services and often
have specialised fit-outs.
Benefits
Higher Rental Yields
Capital Appreciation
Diversification and Professionalism - Allows investors to diversify away from residential
homes. Many commercial tenants are businesses, which can lead to more structured lease
agreements and professional management practices.

[page 6]
Direct investments - Investors can buy full commercial units such as offices, shops or
warehouses in their own name. This requires higher capital and active involvement in
tenant selection, documentation and maintenance. It also concentrates risk in a few large
properties.
REITs (Real Estate Investment Trusts) - REITs pool money from many investors to buy and
manage large commercial portfolios like office parks. Units are listed and traded on stock
exchanges, providing liquidity and lower entry amounts. They distribute a major part of
their income as dividends to unitholders.
Crowdfunding and Fractional Platforms - Some platforms allow investors to buy small
fractions of commercial properties. This reduces ticket size and can give access to
institutional-grade assets. Investors should review legal structures, fees and governance
before committing money.
34.1 - Investment Options in Real Estate
Real Estate & Gold 6
Investment Methods in India
Research and Due Diligence - Before investing, it is important to study location, tenant
profile, lease terms and vacancy levels. Investors should also review building quality, legal
title, approvals and maintenance arrangements.
Private Equity Real Estate Funds - These are professionally managed funds that invest in
multiple commercial projects. They usually target long-term capital growth and may have

ts.
Private Equity Real Estate Funds - These are professionally managed funds that invest in
multiple commercial projects. They usually target long-term capital growth and may have
lock-in periods. Such options are more suited to high-net-worth investors who understand
illiquidity and risk.
Pre-Investment Considerations
Risk–Reward Assessment - CRE returns can fluctuate with the business cycle, interest rates
and local oversupply. Properties may remain vacant between leases, affecting cash flow.
Investors must ensure they can handle such periods without stressing their personal
finances.

[page 7]
Land
Agricultural Land - Agricultural land is legally earmarked for farming and related rural
activities such as growing crops, plantations or keeping livestock. Construction of houses
or commercial buildings is generally not allowed unless the land is formally converted by
the local authorities. In several Indian states, only farmers or people meeting specific state
conditions can directly purchase such land.
Non-Agricultural Land - Non-agricultural land is land that has been approved for uses other
than farming, such as residential, commercial, industrial or institutional projects. It usually
comes with permissions for construction and often has better access to roads, electricity,
water & other civic services. Because it is already converted, it is more suitable for building
homes or business properties, but it also attracts higher prices, taxes & charges.
34.1 - Investment Options in Real Estate
Real Estate & Gold 7
Land as an investment refers to buying a piece of earth without
any major constructed building on it. It can be held for future
development, farming, or simply for resale at a higher price. For
many Indian families, land is seen as a symbol of security and
legacy. It is also viewed as a way to participate in long-term
development of a city, town or village.
Types of Land Investments
Preferred Investment

en as a symbol of security and
legacy. It is also viewed as a way to participate in long-term
development of a city, town or village.
Types of Land Investments
Preferred Investment
Many Indians favour real estate, and land often ranks high because it is tangible and limited in
supply. It is perceived to offer strong resale potential when development reaches the area.
Maintenance expenses are generally low compared with built properties, as there are no
structures to repair.
For some investors, land also represents flexibility. They can decide later whether to build, lease
or sell, depending on family needs and market conditions.
Caution Advised
Buying land requires careful legal and financial evaluation. Title clarity, past ownership, zoning,
and any disputes must be thoroughly checked before payment. Encroachments and unclear
records are common risks.
Investors should also understand local rules on land conversion, stamp duty and capital gains
tax. Limited availability, infrastructure delays or policy changes can slow price growth.

[page 8]
Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs)
34.1 - Investment Options in Real Estate
Real Estate & Gold 8
REITs are investment vehicles that own or manage a portfolio
of income-generating real estate. They allow investors to
participate in large commercial properties without directly
buying buildings. In India, listed REITs mainly focus on
offices, with growing interest in other segments. For many
households, REITs provide a bridge between real estate and
traditional market investments like equity funds.
Real Estate Ownership
REITs own, operate, or finance income-generating commercial real estate properties, such as
office spaces, malls, hotel, etc.
The properties in a REIT are managed by experienced real estate professionals. They handle
leasing, maintenance and upgrades to keep occupancy and rents healthy. This structure lets
investors benefit from real estate returns without day-to-day operational responsibilities.
Features of REITs
Proportionate Ownership - When an investor buys REIT units, they get a proportional claim
on the underlying portfolio & its income. The units trade on stock exchanges, so prices move
like shares. This makes it easier to enter or exit compared with directly selling a property.
Equity-like Instrument - Regulations treat listed REIT units as equity securities, not as

e shares. This makes it easier to enter or exit compared with directly selling a property.
Equity-like Instrument - Regulations treat listed REIT units as equity securities, not as
physical property. Investors can receive both rental income (through distributions) and
potential capital gains if unit prices rise. At the same time, prices can fall with market
conditions and real estate cycles.
Funds Pooling Mechanism
Pooling of Investor Money - REITs collect money from many investors, including individuals
and institutions. This pooled capital is used to acquire, develop or refinance multiple
commercial properties. Spreading investments across many tenants and buildings reduces
dependence on any single asset.
Diversified Real Estate Portfolio - Because of pooling, even a small investor can gain
exposure to a large, diversified portfolio. The REIT may own properties in different cities,
micro-markets and tenant industries. This diversification can help smooth income and
reduce specific property risk.

[page 9]
Stock Exchanges and Mutual Funds - Retail investors can buy or sell listed REIT units
through normal stock-broking accounts, similar to equity shares. Some mutual funds also
invest in REITs, offering indirect access through fund schemes. Liquidity depends on trading
volumes in the market.
IPOs and follow-on Issues - New REITs may first raise money through an initial public
offering (IPO). Existing REITs can also raise additional funds via follow-on offerings.
Personal Finance Professionals can help clients decide how much to allocate to REITs based
on risk profile, income needs and overall asset mix.
34.1 - Investment Options in Real Estate
Real Estate & Gold 9
Investment Avenues
How REITs works?
Fractional Ownership
Fractional ownership in real estate allows
multiple investors to jointly own a single
high-value property. Each investor buys a
defined share instead of the entire property.
This model is becoming popular in India for
Grade-A offices, warehouses and holiday
homes that would otherwise be out of reach
for individual investors.
For Personal Finance Professionals, it opens another route to add real estate exposure with
lower ticket sizes.

[page 10]
Shared Ownership Structure - Under fractional ownership, a property is legally held in a
structure where many investors participate together. Each person contributes a part of the
total purchase cost. Rental income and eventual sale proceeds are shared in proportion to
their holding.
Ownership Percentage & Usage Rights - Every investor holds a clear ownership percentage,
documented through units, shares or agreements. Their income entitlement and voting
rights are linked to this proportion.
34.1 - Investment Options in Real Estate
Real Estate & Gold 10
Key Features
Expense & Maintenance Sharing - All regular expenses such as maintenance, insurance,
repairs and property management fees are shared by investors. The split usually matches
each investor’s ownership percentage.
Flexibility in Sale - After an initial lock-in, investors can usually sell their fractional interest
without selling the whole property. The exit may be through a platform marketplace, private
transfer or a structured buy-back.
Advantages and Disadvantages of Fractional Ownership
Advantages
Lower ticket size to access high-value properties
Diversification across multiple assets instead of one property
Professional property and tenant management
Potential for regular rental income
Possibility of capital appreciation on underlying asset
Shared maintenance and operating costs
Disadvantages

onal property and tenant management
Potential for regular rental income
Possibility of capital appreciation on underlying asset
Shared maintenance and operating costs
Disadvantages
Limited control over property-level decisions
Liquidity can be low; exit may take time
Platform / management fees reduce net returns
Conflicts possible among multiple co-owners
Regulatory and legal structures still evolving in India
Rental income and prices depend on market conditions

[page 11]
Buying property without a clear goal, budget and time frame often leads to stress later.
Emotional pressure from family, friends or trends can push investors into choices that do not
fit their finances.
Many investors skip basic checks on location, demand, rental yields and future supply.
Without this homework, they risk buying in areas with weak growth or poor resale
potential.
34.1 - Investment Options in Real Estate
Real Estate & Gold 11
Mistakes Investors Make with Real Estate
Real estate is generally a long-term asset, but some buyers expect quick profits. Short
holding periods can make returns low after costs like stamp duty, brokerage and taxes.
In a hurry to close a deal, investors may accept inflated prices without independent
valuation. Overpaying reduces future returns and can delay breakeven for many years.
Owners often ignore costs such as major repairs, society charges, vacancy and legal fees.
These surprise outflows strain cash flows and can force distress sales or extra borrowing.
Changes in job, health or income can make EMIs or maintenance difficult to manage. A
backup plan such as emergency funds protects the family if things go wrong.
Many people decide to buy only because others say “rent is waste” without comparing
numbers. A calm rent-vs-buy analysis, aligned to goals and stability, leads to better
decisions.

[page 12]
Learning Objective Coverage:
34.2
Risks involved in Real Estate Investment
34.2 - Risk-Return Profile of Real Estate
Risk-Return Profile of Real Estate
Risks involved in Real Estate Investment
Real Estate Investment - Returns
Real Estate & Gold 12
Real Estate can be a powerful wealth-building tool, but every
property investment carries specific risks. Understanding these
risks helps investors avoid unpleasant surprises and plan better
cash flows. PFPs should highlight these areas so that clients enter
deals with realistic expectations, not just return projections.
Financial Risk - This arises when buyers use loans and are exposed to changing
interest rates and EMI burdens. If income falls or rates rise, it can become difficult
to service the debt and hold the property.
Liquidity Risk - Property usually cannot be sold quickly without compromising on
price. In weak markets or niche locations, finding a serious buyer can take
months.
Management Risk - Real estate needs regular upkeep, tenant management and
documentation. Poor maintenance or weak tenant selection can reduce rent,
increase vacancies and hurt overall returns.
Regulatory Risk - Changes in government regulations, zoning norms, building by-
laws, taxation and land-use policies.
Legal Risk - Risks arising from defective property titles, litigation, non-compliance
with regulations, approvals and disputes.

[page 13]
Real Estate Investment - Returns
From 2002–2012, annual returns were largely in low- to mid-double digits, with years like
2005, 2007 and 2010 showing gains of 22–24%, resulting in a very strong compound
growth rate (CAGR) of about 15% for that phase.
In the later period, 2013–2025, yearly returns dropped to mostly mid-single digits, with
several years (2015, 2017, 2020) close to 0–3%, bringing the phase CAGR down to around
5%.
When both periods are combined, the overall 2002–2025 CAGR for the housing index
works out to roughly 10%, indicating that long-term Indian residential property has
delivered reasonable but slowing price appreciation over the last two decades. 
34.2 - Risk-Return Profile of Real Estate
Real Estate & Gold 13
The above data shows calendar-year returns from 2002 to 2025 YTD for Indian residential real
estate, and splits this into two clear cycles.
Environmental Risk - Location-related issues such as flooding, pollution, zoning
changes or infrastructure projects can affect livability and values. Investors must
study these factors early to avoid long-term damage to returns.
Source: NHB, Indiabudget.gov.in. Returns are calculated based on NHB Residex. Returns are updated till Dec’25.

[page 14]

34.3
34.3 - Investment Options in Gold
Investment Options in Gold
Why Investment in Gold?
Investment Options in Gold
Mistakes Investors Make with Gold
Real Estate & Gold 14
Why Investment in Gold?
Gold is a long-standing store of value for Indian households,
held both as jewellery and as an investment asset. Gold is
one of the most preferred investments in India. Over the
past 20–30 years, it has delivered competitive returns in
many periods while also acting as a hedge in crises.
Diverse / Emotional Appeal - Gold’s price is driven not only by investment demand but also
by jewellery, central bank buying and industrial use. These multiple demand sources make it
behave differently from traditional financial assets in many market conditions.
Effective Diversification - Gold usually has low or negative correlation with equities and, at
times, with currencies and bonds. Adding a sensible allocation can reduce overall portfolio
volatility without relying on short-term market timing.
Safe Haven - During economic or geopolitical stress, investors worldwide often move
money into gold. This shift can support prices when riskier assets such as equities are
falling, offering some protection to the overall portfolio.
Currency Hedge - Gold is priced globally in US dollars and typically rises when major

iskier assets such as equities are
falling, offering some protection to the overall portfolio.
Currency Hedge - Gold is priced globally in US dollars and typically rises when major
currencies weaken or inflation worries increase. For Indian investors, this can partly offset
the impact of rupee depreciation over long horizons.
Risk-Adjusted Enhancement - Because of its diversification benefits, a measured gold
allocation can improve risk-adjusted returns rather than just chasing higher returns.

[page 15]
Physical Gold
Physical gold provides the most direct exposure to gold.
Gold in bulk form is referred to as bullion, and it can be cast
into bars or minted into coins. Gold bullion’s value is based
on its mass and purity rather than monetary face value. Even
if a gold coin is issued with a monetary face value, its market
value is tied to the value of its fine gold content.
34.3 - Investment Options in Gold
Real Estate & Gold 15
Investors can buy physical gold from government mints, private mints, precious metals
dealers, and jewellers. Because different sellers may offer the exact same item at different
prices, it is important to do your research to find the best deal. When you purchase
physical gold, you must pay the full price.
Physical gold ownership involves a number of costs, including storage and insurance costs,
and the transaction fees and markups associated with buying and selling the commodity.
There can also be processing fees and small-lot fees for investors making limited
purchases. While collectively these costs may not significantly affect someone looking to
invest a small portion of their portfolio in gold, the costs may become prohibitive for
investors seeking to gain larger exposure.
Investment Options in Gold
Gold based ETFs
Structure - Gold ETFs are traded on stock exchanges and represent ownership in gold

bitive for
investors seeking to gain larger exposure.
Investment Options in Gold
Gold based ETFs
Structure - Gold ETFs are traded on stock exchanges and represent ownership in gold
backed by 99.5% pure physical gold bars. This setup makes it easy for investors to get
exposure to gold’s price movement without owning actual metal.
Risk Consideration - Gold ETFs’ value can fluctuate due to changes in market gold prices.
This means that investors may see ups and downs in their investment value, based on
global factors affecting gold rates.
A Gold based Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs) invests in gold bullion
and aims to track the performance of the price of gold. The units
of these ETFs are traded on stock exchanges and can be bought
and sold like any other stock. Instead of buying gold in physical
form, one can invest in gold digitally through these ETFs.

[page 16]
Real Estate & Gold 16
Suitability - Gold ETFs are suitable for those who want to invest in gold without worrying
about risks like theft, purity, or storage. They provide a convenient and low-cost way to
own gold through an electronic format. This works well for investors who prefer paperless
investments and easy access without dealing with physical gold.
Accessibility of Investment - Gold ETFs can only be bought in demat (electronic) form, so
investors don’t receive any physical gold. This is especially convenient for small investors,
making it easy to buy or sell even a tiny amount via online trading accounts.
34.3 - Investment Options in Gold
Gold Based Mutual Funds
Flexible Investment Amount - Gold mutual funds offer greater convenience than physical
gold as it allows an investor to purchase any amount of funds as per their requirement. One
can invest as low as Rs.1000, which allows individuals with low income to invest in this type
of fund.
Gold based funds are mutual funds that invest primarily in Gold
Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs). These funds don’t invest in physical
gold directly, but they track the price of gold through these ETFs.
Gold
Mutual Funds
Gold mutual funds are open-ended investments, based on the units provided by the Gold ETFs.
Instead of purchasing physical gold, which often carries a significant high cost, it offers

d mutual funds are open-ended investments, based on the units provided by the Gold ETFs.
Instead of purchasing physical gold, which often carries a significant high cost, it offers
more flexibility to an investor.
Highly Liquid Investment - Another major advantage of a gold mutual fund is that it can be
liquidated on short notice and without much hassle. Trading these funds is easier than
liquidating other types of assets, which makes them ideal as a financial cushion to protect
against an unforeseen incident.
Also, there is no lower limit on the redeemable amounts, allowing an individual to redeem
according to their unique financial requirements.
Diversify Investment Portfolio - Gold mutual funds are an excellent investment options to
diversify one’s investment portfolio and reduce overall market risk. As a physical asset, gold
prices are not directly related to company stocks. 
Safer than owning Physical Gold - Gold mutual funds are electronic investments, which
eliminate the hassle of storing physical gold. For purchase both the forms are available -
Demat and Non-demat.

[page 17]
Sovereign Gold Bonds
Gold Denomination - Sovereign Gold Bonds are securities issued by the government that
represent units of gold, rather than physical gold itself. This means the bond's value is
measured in grams of gold, allowing investors to track gold prices without handling actual
metal.
Government Issued - Sovereign Gold Bonds are issued by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI)
on behalf of the Government of India. This ensures that the investment is backed by the
central government, making it secure and reliable.
Real Estate & Gold 17
Sovereign Gold Bonds (SGBs) are government-backed financial
instruments that let investors gain exposure to gold without having
to buy or store physical gold. They are designed as a convenient,
tax-efficient and secure alternative to traditional gold investments.
Eligible Investors - A wide range of entities can invest in Sovereign Gold Bonds, including
individuals, Hindu Undivided Families (HUFs), trusts, universities, and charitable institutions.
Investment Limits - Investors must buy at least 1 gram of gold through these bonds, with a
maximum limit of 4 kilograms per person in a financial year. This ceiling includes both
primary issuances and secondary market purchases but does not count any gold provided as
bank collateral.
Fixed Interest Rate - Sovereign Gold Bonds offer a fixed annual interest rate of 2.50%,

nces and secondary market purchases but does not count any gold provided as
bank collateral.
Fixed Interest Rate - Sovereign Gold Bonds offer a fixed annual interest rate of 2.50%,
which is paid out twice a year to the investor. The final interest payment is made at
maturity along with the redemption amount. This fixed return is in addition to any gains
from the appreciation in gold prices, providing both steady income and capital growth
potential.
34.3 - Investment Options in Gold
Taxation - The interest earned from Sovereign Gold Bonds is fully taxable, meaning
investors must include it in their income and pay tax as per their income tax slab. However,
if the bonds are held till maturity (usually eight years), the capital gains, profit from the
appreciation in gold value are exempt from tax.
Trading Market - Sovereign Gold Bonds are listed on the stock exchange, which means they
can be bought or sold in the secondary market after their initial issue. This gives investors
the flexibility to exit or enter at any time before maturity, based on market liquidity.

[page 18]
Storage Elimination - Investing in Sovereign Gold Bonds means there is no need to worry
about storing physical gold, which can be risky and expensive. These bonds are held in
demat or certificate form, so theft, loss, or storage costs are eliminated.
Electronic Gold Receipts (EGR)
What Are EGRs - EGRs are tradable securities representing gold of a fixed purity, held in
SEBI-accredited vaults. This eliminates the need for an investor to physically store gold.
Real Estate & Gold 18
The Reserve Bank of India has currently stopped issuing new Sovereign Gold Bonds. Investors can
still trade existing SGBs in the secondary market and continue to hold the bonds already
purchased until maturity.
34.3 - Investment Options in Gold
Electronic Gold Receipts (EGR) are SEBI-regulated, exchange
traded instruments that let investors buy, hold, and trade gold in
electronic form backed by physical gold in accredited vaults
without holding the physical gold themselves.
Exchange-Traded - EGRs are held in demat form and traded on NSE and BSE like regular
stocks. Investors can buy, sell, or hold them with the same ease and liquidity as equities.
Convertibility - Investors can convert their EGR holding into physical gold, or convert
physical gold into an EGR, through SEBI-registered Vault Managers. This two-way

as equities.
Convertibility - Investors can convert their EGR holding into physical gold, or convert
physical gold into an EGR, through SEBI-registered Vault Managers. This two-way
convertibility is what distinguishes EGRs from other paper-gold products like ETFs.
Key Participants - The ecosystem involves four parties: the Vault Manager (stores the gold),
the Depository (holds EGRs in demat form), the Exchange (facilitates trading), and the
Investor/Broker (buys and sells).

[page 19]
Real Estate & Gold 19
Investing without purpose - Many people buy gold without a clear reason, often because it
feels safe or because others are doing it. Knowing the purpose -whether for protection,
profit, or savings helps match investment to financial goals.
Superficial view of diversification - Some investors think gold always moves opposite to
stocks or the dollar, but this isn’t true in every situation. Gold can rise or fall in both bull and
bear markets, so it’s better to see gold as one part of overall returns rather than as the only
protection in the portfolio.
Ignoring intrinsic value vs. market price - Many buy gold thinking only about its price in
rupees or dollars, forgetting its real value and what happens in the long term. Changes in
currencies and economies can affect gold’s worth differently, so it’s important to consider
both short-term price and long-term buying power.
Treating gold as a short-term bet - Gold is usually better for long-term holding, as its price
can go up and down quickly in the short term. Selling too soon can result in losses; patience
is needed to benefit from gold’s steady increase over years.
Buying at the wrong time - Gold prices fluctuate, and buying when prices are high or during
panic can lead to losses. It’s smarter to research trends and buy when the market is

rs.
Buying at the wrong time - Gold prices fluctuate, and buying when prices are high or during
panic can lead to losses. It’s smarter to research trends and buy when the market is
favorable, rather than following the crowd or reacting emotionally.
Letting emotions drive decisions - Fear or excitement often causes investors to buy or sell
gold hastily. Rational decisions based on goals and research are safer for investment
success.
34.3 - Investment Options in Gold
Mistakes Investors Make with Gold

[page 20]
Learning Objective Coverage:
34.4
Risks involved in Gold Investment
34.4 - Risk-Return Profile of Gold
Risk-Return Profile of Gold
Risks involved in Gold Investment
Gold Investment - Returns
Real Estate & Gold 20
Gold can play an important role in the portfolios, but it is not risk-free.
PFPs need to highlight these risks so that clients use gold in the right
proportion and with realistic expectations.
Price Volatility - Gold prices can move sharply in short periods due to global sentiment,
currency moves and central-bank actions. Such swings can lead to interim losses if investors
are forced to sell at the wrong time.
Opportunity Cost - Gold does not generate regular income such as interest, dividends or rental
income.
Economic and Geo-Political Risk - Major political or policy events such as import duty changes
or restrictions on gold flows can influence prices and liquidity.
Storage and Insurance Costs - Physical gold must be stored safely in lockers or vaults and may
need insurance cover. These annual costs eat into overall returns, especially when price growth
is modest.
Purity and Authenticity Risk - Risks include adulterated purity, fake hallmarking, or scams in
digital and scheme-based gold products. Dealing only with reputed, regulated entities and
insisting on proper documentation helps reduce this risk.

[page 21]
Gold Investment - Returns
Over 40 years, gold has delivered healthy annualised returns of about 12%, with 10-, 20- and
30-year periods in the graphic showing roughly 16%, 14% and 12% returns respectively. 
Large parts of the 1980–1989, 1996–2002 and 2012–2019 phases show almost 0% price
growth, meaning investors who bought at the start of these windows saw little gain for
many years. 
In contrast, powerful bull runs 1989–1996 at about 12% CAGR, 2002–2012 at around 19%
CAGR, and the recent 2019–2026 phase at roughly 21% CAGR—have driven most of the
long-term wealth creation.
34.4 - Risk-Return Profile of Gold
Real Estate & Gold 21
The above data highlights that how gold returns have come in distinct cycles rather than in a
straight line.

B6=1a) · C6=Rohan and Meera are planning to purchase a residential property in 2026. They are evaluating whether they should buy the house immediately or continue staying on rent for a few years and postpone the purchase decision.

They have shortlisted a property currently valued at ₹92,00,000. If they buy now, they will make a 25% down payment and Rohan take an individual home loan for the balance amount. Passive investing means replicating a market index like Nifty 50 or Sensex by investing in the
same stocks and proportions. The passive funds track the index’s performance instead of trying
to beat it. Fund managers make minimal decisions and only adjust the portfolio to match the
index. There is no active stock selection or research involved.
Active and passive management differ by how much the fund manager controls buying and
selling. Active funds involve frequent decisions and analysis, while passive funds simply follow
a market index.
Active vs Passive
Actively Managed Portfolio
Here, the fund manager studies markets and chooses assets to
outperform benchmarks. They adjust holdings based on performance
and economic trends, aiming for higher returns.
Passively Managed Portfolio
In contrast, a passively managed portfolio, often associated with
Exchange-Traded Funds (ETFs), tracks the performance of a
specific index without active decision-making by a fund manager.
The manager only updates holdings when the index changes.

Exchange-Traded Funds (ETFs), tracks the performance of a
specific index without active decision-making by a fund manager.
The manager only updates holdings when the index changes.
Returns mirror the index’s performance, minus small costs or fees.

[page 4]
Advantages of Passive Funds
Lower Management Fees - Passive funds track an index like Nifty or Sensex, so costs for
research and trading are low, leading to cheaper management fees.
No Active Stock Selection - Managers don’t pick stocks manually; the fund mirrors the
index, reducing human error and biased decisions.
Minimal Research - Since the fund follows an index, limited analysis is needed, making it
simple, transparent, and aligned with market performance.
Passive Strategies - These funds use a long-term buy-and-hold method, avoiding frequent
trading or market timing, ideal for hands-off investors.

Types of Passive Funds
Exchange Traded
Funds (ETFs)
ETFs, are investment products that trade on stock exchanges
using Demat accounts. They follow an index and their price
changes throughout the trading day, similar to common stocks.
ETFs offer transparency, low costs, and diversification, but if few
people buy or sell them, it may affect prices and returns. Fund
houses (AMCs) help maintain liquidity, but low volumes can
make buying and selling costlier. Overall, ETFs are a passive and
efficient way to invest in the market.
Index Funds
Index Funds are mutual funds that also aim to mirror a market
index, such as the Nifty or Sensex, by investing in the same
stocks and proportions as the index. Unlike ETFs, you buy or sell
index funds at the end-of-day price, not during market hours.

Passive Funds - Categories
1) Asset Based
Equity
Equity-based passive funds are designed to replicate the performance
of a stock market index such as the Nifty 50 ETF, Sensex Index, or
Nifty Next 50 Index.
Debt
Debt-based passive funds aim to track the performance of a basket of
fixed-income securities, such as government bonds, PSU debt, or other
high-grade instruments. A common example is the Bharat Bond ETF,
which follows a target maturity structure and includes bonds issued by
government-owned entities.
State Development Loan (SDL) ETFs - Invest in bonds issued by
state governments.
Bond ETFs - These trade like shares on the stock market and invest
only in bonds, so investor can buy and sell easily.
Gilt ETFs - Invest solely in government bonds.
Liquid
Liquid-based passive funds invest in short-term money market
instruments, including treasury bills, government securities, and
commercial papers. These instruments are selected based on their
short maturity periods and high credit quality. The fund’s objective is
to mirror the returns of the liquid market segment while ensuring high
liquidity and capital preservation. E.g. Liquid BeEs.
Commodities
Commodity-based passive funds are structured to track the market

of the liquid market segment while ensuring high
liquidity and capital preservation. E.g. Liquid BeEs.
Commodities
Commodity-based passive funds are structured to track the market
price of physical commodities like gold and silver. These funds usually
hold the commodity in physical or dematerialized form and adjust their
holdings to match the spot price or a relevant commodity index. E.g.
Gold ETF, Gold MF & Silver ETF.

[page 7]
35.1 - Passive Funds
Other Products - Passive Funds, International Investment, MSB, etc 7
2) Broad Market Based
Large + Mid + Small Cap
This category includes indices that represent the entire listed
equity market by combining companies across all market
capitalizations—large, mid, and small caps. E.g. Nifty 500 Index.
Large & Mid Cap Blend
This type includes indices that focus specifically on large-cap
and mid-cap companies, excluding small-cap firms. E.g. Nifty
Large&Mid Cap 250 Index.
3) Market Cap Based
Large Cap
Large-cap based passive funds track indices that include the
top 100 listed companies by market capitalization. E.g. Nifty 50
Index, Nifty 100 ETF.
Mid Cap
Mid-cap passive indices consist of companies ranked roughly
between 101st and 250th by market capitalization. E.g. Nifty
Midcap 150 Index.
Small Cap
Small-cap indices represent companies beyond the top 250 in
market capitalization. E.g. Nifty Small Cap 250 Index.
4) Sectoral/ Thematic
Sectoral
Sectoral passive funds track indices focused on a specific
sector of the economy, such as IT, banking, or pharma. E.g.
Nifty IT ETF, Nifty Pharma Index.
Thematic
Thematic passive funds go beyond sectors and instead focus
on investment themes that cut across sectors. These themes
could be consumption, infrastructure, ESG, or digital trends.
E.g. Nifty India Consumption ETF.

[page 8]
35.1 - Passive Funds
Other Products - Passive Funds, International Investment, MSB, etc 8
5) Factor/ Smart Beta
Equal Weight
Equal weight indices assign equal importance to all constituent
stocks, regardless of their market capitalization. For example, in
the Nifty 50 Equal Weight Index, each of the 50 stocks holds
the same weight in the index. This avoids concentration risk
and gives smaller large-cap companies more influence
compared to traditional market-cap-weighted indices.
Low Volatility
Low volatility passive funds focus on stocks with historically
lower price fluctuations. These indices, such as the Nifty Low
Volatility 30 ETF, include companies that show relatively stable
returns over time, aiming to reduce downside risk and provide
smoother performance during market turbulence.
Alpha + Low Volatility
This strategy combines two factors—alpha generation and low
volatility—in a single index. The Nifty Alpha Low Volatility 30
ETF selects stocks that not only demonstrate consistent
returns above the benchmark (alpha) but also exhibit lower
volatility. It aims to deliver better risk-adjusted returns through
a dual-filter approach.
6) Quality Factor
High ROE/
Low Debt Stocks
Quality factor passive funds focus on fundamentally strong
companies with high return on equity (ROE) and low debt
levels. These companies are considered financially healthy and

ks
Quality factor passive funds focus on fundamentally strong
companies with high return on equity (ROE) and low debt
levels. These companies are considered financially healthy and
capable of generating stable earnings. The Nifty100 Quality 30
Index is an example that includes such stocks selected from
the Nifty 100 universe.

[page 9]
35.1 - Passive Funds
Other Products - Passive Funds, International Investment, MSB, etc 9
7) Value Factor
Undervalued Stocks
Value factor funds aim to identify stocks trading below their
intrinsic value, often using financial ratios like price-to-earnings
or price-to-book. These funds include companies perceived to
be undervalued by the market. The Nifty50 Value 20 Index is
designed to capture the performance of 20 such value stocks
from the Nifty 50.
8) Momentum Factor
Price Performance
Based
Momentum funds select stocks that have shown strong recent
price performance. The idea is that stocks with positive
momentum are likely to continue their trend in the short to
medium term. The Nifty200 Momentum 30 Index includes 30
stocks with high momentum from the Nifty 200 universe.
9) International
US Tech
This sub-type focuses on passive investments tracking the
technology sector of the US market. The Nasdaq 100 Index
includes leading non-financial companies listed on the Nasdaq
exchange, heavily weighted toward tech giants.
US Broad Market
This category represents a diversified set of large-cap US
stocks across various sectors. The S&P 500 Index tracks 500 of
the largest US companies and serves as a benchmark for the
US equity market, providing broad exposure to the American
economy.

Investing in passives can be a strategic and cost-effective way to build a diversified portfolio.
Here are some factors to consider when evaluating Passives:
Key Factors When Choosing Passives
Asset Class as per Client's Asset Allocation and Risk Profile - Consider the client's
investment goals, time horizon, and risk tolerance. Align the ETFs with the desired asset
allocation, whether it's equities, fixed income, commodities, or a mix. Diversify across
different sectors or geographic regions to spread risk.
Passive Versus Managed Funds - Understand whether the client prefers a passive or active
investment strategy. Passive ETFs track a specific index, providing broad market exposure,
while actively managed ETFs involve fund managers making specific investment decisions.
Passive funds often have lower fees, while active funds may aim for outperformance.
Transaction Costs
Brokerage Fees - Evaluate the cost of buying and selling ETFs through a broker. Look for
low-cost brokerage platforms to minimize expenses.
Liquidity Costs - Check the liquidity of the ETF by examining average trading volumes.
More liquid ETFs tend to have smaller bid-ask spreads, reducing transaction costs.
Management Fees - Understand the expense ratio, which includes management fees.

trading volumes.
More liquid ETFs tend to have smaller bid-ask spreads, reducing transaction costs.
Management Fees - Understand the expense ratio, which includes management fees.
Lower expense ratios are generally favourable for investors.
Tracking Errors
Assess how closely the ETF tracks its underlying index.
A low tracking error indicates that the fund closely follows the index performance.
Factors contributing to tracking errors include management decisions, transaction costs,
and the efficiency of the ETF's replication strategy.

International investing refers to the act of investing money in foreign
countries and the markets of those countries, such as stocks, bonds,
real estate, and other financial instruments. This type of investing is
an opportunity for investors to diversify their portfolios, tap into the
growth potential of economies and companies in other countries, and
potentially benefit from different market conditions and currencies. 
However, it also comes with additional risks, such as currency fluctuations, political instability,
and different legal and regulatory frameworks. As with any type of investing, international
investing requires careful research and consideration of one's investment goals and risk
tolerance before making any decisions.

[page 13]
For Indian investors, international investing offers exposure to developed economies like
the US, Europe, and Japan, providing access to companies operating in mature and stable
markets. This exposure can complement domestic investments and provide opportunities
for growth that may not be available solely within India's market.
International investing allows investors to purchase fractional shares of companies, enabling
them to invest in high-priced stocks with smaller amounts of capital. This accessibility
broadens investment opportunities and allows for more precise allocation of funds across
different assets.
Investing internationally can hedge against the risks of depreciation in the Indian rupee
(INR) against foreign currencies. Holding investments denominated in foreign currencies
can act as a natural hedge, as fluctuations in exchange rates may offset losses in domestic
currency value, providing a measure of protection for investors' portfolios.
Source – Axis MF
35.2 - International Investments
Other Products - Passive Funds, International Investment, MSB, etc 13
It is true that Indian investors tend to have a higher home bias compared to investors in other
countries. Home bias refers to the tendency for investors to prefer investing in their domestic
markets and companies, rather than investing internationally. This can limit the diversification

ome bias refers to the tendency for investors to prefer investing in their domestic
markets and companies, rather than investing internationally. This can limit the diversification
of their portfolios and potentially reduce their overall returns.
International stocks introduce diversification by exposing investors to different economies,
industries, and currencies. This diversification can help mitigate risks associated with
fluctuations in domestic markets and reduce overall portfolio volatility.
Investing internationally provides access to renowned and respected growth firms that may
not be available in domestic markets. Companies like Apple, Amazon, or Alibaba offer
opportunities for growth and profitability that can enhance a portfolio's performance.
Why International Investing?
Home Bias of Indian Investors, Higher Than Other Geographies

[page 14]
Familiarity Bias - The investor trusts what feels known, favoring domestic companies and
markets over unfamiliar global ones simply because they're easier to relate to.
35.2 - International Investments
Other Products - Passive Funds, International Investment, MSB, etc 14
Factors Contributing to Home Bias for Investors & PFPs
There are several factors contributing to home bias for investors and PFPs, including:
Currency-linked Decision Making – Since the investor's income and financial goals are
denominated in INR, investment choices naturally default toward INR-denominated assets
to avoid currency mismatch.
Cost of Accessing Global Markets – Higher fees, added documentation, and unfamiliar
platforms make overseas investing feel more cumbersome and less accessible to the investor.
Regulatory Ambiguity – Frequently evolving or unclear compliance norms around overseas
investing (LRS limits, tax treatment, reporting) create hesitation for the investor.
Return Expectations – Hindsight bias from strong past performance leads the investor to
expect higher future returns from domestic markets than global ones.
Can diversify return sources by allocating a portion to global markets, smoothing out
returns instead of depending solely on domestic performance.
Framework for Addressing Home-Country Bias

sify return sources by allocating a portion to global markets, smoothing out
returns instead of depending solely on domestic performance.
Framework for Addressing Home-Country Bias
While home-country bias feels natural, a structured framework helps the investor decide how
much global diversification actually makes sense for their portfolio.
Can mitigate concentration risk by reducing over-reliance on a single economy and currency
(INR), spreading exposure across geographies.
Can address market valuation gaps by allocating globally when domestic markets are
trading at expensive valuations relative to global peers.
Should evaluate costs and liquidity, factoring in taxes (like TCS on LRS remittances),
transaction charges, and access constraints before investing abroad.
Ultimately, addressing home-country bias isn't about abandoning domestic markets, but about
making a deliberate, well-evaluated choice to include global exposure where it adds value.
Should assess macro and policy risks, including political developments, regulatory changes,
and geopolitical tensions that could affect global holdings.

[page 15]
Merits and Demerits of International Investment

Investment in global blue chips stocks such as Apple, Microsoft, Tesla, Amazon and

High-yield bonds are a type of debt security that offers a higher yield than traditional bonds.
These bonds are issued by companies that are considered to be prone to risk, and they typically
have a lower credit rating than investment-grade bonds.
High-yield bonds are often used by companies to finance expansion or other capital expenditures.
They are also used by investors who are seeking a higher return on their investment.
Features of High Yield Corporate Debt
Higher Interest Rates - High yield bonds offer higher interest rates than investment-grade
bonds to compensate for their higher risk. These bonds can offer even higher rates.
Higher Volatility - High yield bonds are more volatile than investment-grade bonds and can
experience price fluctuations in response to changes in the issuing company's
creditworthiness or market conditions.

Lower Credit Ratings - Bonds that offer high yields are often issued by companies with less-
than-stellar credit ratings, so they offer higher yields than bonds from more creditworthy
companies. Therefore, interest payments and principal repayments may not be made.
Potentially Higher Returns - High yield bonds have the potential to offer higher returns than
investment-grade bonds due to their higher interest rates.

Credit Rating of High Yield Bonds
High yield bonds usually have a lower credit rating (typically in the range of A+ to BBB). These
ratings are given by credit rating agencies such as CRISIL, ICRA, CARE, etc. As a result, they
compensate the lower credit rating with higher yield and higher coupon rate.
AAA: highest degree of safety, lowest credit risk
AA-, AA, AA+: high degree of safety, very low credit risk
A-, A, A+: adequate degree of safety, low credit risk
BBB-, BBB, BBB+: Moderate degree of safety, moderate credit risk
BB: Moderate risk of default
B-, B, B+: high risk of default
C: very high risk of default
D: In default or expected to be in default
Invoice Discounting
It is a form of financing chosen by businesses to tap into their unpaid invoices so that they can
meet their working capital requirements. Essentially, it is post-sales funding. Businesses avail
financing towards unpaid invoices for the goods already delivered at a pre-determined cost.
High ROE - Invoice discounting can yield 10–15% p.a., much higher than FDs or short-term
debt funds. For instance, a business on platforms like CredAble or TradeCred may pay a
12% annualized rate to get early payment for its ₹50 lakh invoice to Tata Motors. Investors

debt funds. For instance, a business on platforms like CredAble or TradeCred may pay a
12% annualized rate to get early payment for its ₹50 lakh invoice to Tata Motors. Investors
earn this attractive return due to the company’s willingness to pay for faster liquidity.
Features of Invoice Discounting
Investment Period - The tenure of invoice discounting usually ranges between 30–90 days.
For example, an investor could fund an invoice raised by an MSME supplying packaging
material to ITC Ltd for 90 days through KredX. Once ITC pays the invoice, the investor
receives both principal and interest, making it ideal for short-term cash parking.
Diversification - Invoice discounting offers exposure to multiple industries and clients. For
example, investors can fund invoices raised by vendors to Marico, Flipkart, and L&T on
platforms like Oxyzo. Each deal has a different business, sector, and tenor, helping spread
risk and improve portfolio stability within the debt allocation.
Low Correlation with Equity - Returns from invoice discounting depend on invoice
repayments, not stock market movements. For instance, even if the Nifty 50 drops by 10%,
an investor financing invoices of a vendor to Hindustan Unilever (HUL) through GrowFix
would still earn steady returns, since payment is tied to HUL’s credit cycle, not market trends.

[page 22]

22
Credit rating companies, before giving any rating to a company, they consider many factors, but
the broad parameters are 4C’s of credit – Character, Capacity, Capital and Collateral.
1. Character - Character refers to the financial history of the borrower. Character is most often
determined by looking at the credit history, particularly as it is stated in the credit score. 
Factors that will affect the credit score include, the fewer the
problems, the higher the credit score. A high credit score (over
700) may be the most important factor in getting a business
loan. Some factors that affect credit score include – Late
payments, Available credit and Total debt.
Business and personal credit are two different things. Most new businesses have no business
credit, so they must use the personal credit of their owners. In such situations as business loans
and leases, the owner may need to give a personal guarantee.
2. Capacity - Capacity refers to the ability of the business to generate
revenues to pay back the loan. Since a new business has no "track
record" of profits, it is riskiest for a bank to consider. If person is
buying a business, capacity is easier to determine, and a business that
can show a positive cash flow (where income exceeds expenses) for a
sustained period of time has a good chance of getting a business loan.

easier to determine, and a business that
can show a positive cash flow (where income exceeds expenses) for a
sustained period of time has a good chance of getting a business loan.
3. Capital - Capital refers to the capital assets of the business. Capital
assets might include machinery and equipment for a manufacturing
company, as well as product inventory or store or other fixtures. 
Banks consider capital, but with some reluctance, because if your
business folds, they are left with assets that have depreciated and they
must find someplace to sell these assets, at liquidation value. You can
see why a bank considers cash the best asset.
4. Collateral - Collateral is the cash and assets a business owner
pledges to secure a loan. In addition to having good credit, a proven
ability to make money and business assets, banks will often require an
owner to pledge their own personal assets as security for the loan.

Meaning
An increase in a capital assets value during its holding period. It is realized when you sell the

Capital Gains Tax
Meaning
It is the tax you pay on the profit made from selling assets like property, bonds or stocks. The
tax rate depends on how long you held the asset (short or long-term).
A capital gain is when individuals or corporations sell an investment or an asset for a profit.
When they realize a capital gain, the proceeds are considered taxable income.
The amount they owe in capital gains taxes depends in part on how long they owned the
asset.
It is realized when they sell the asset and must be shown as income in the Income tax
declaration.

Any profit or gain that arises from the sale or transfer of a "capital asset" by a taxpayer during a

of management or control of an Indian company.

Any amount received by a nominee on the death of the life insured under a ULIP is fully exempt

Maturity Proceeds
The tax treatment of maturity proceeds depends on the issue date and the premium paid:
For ULIPs issued on or after 1 February 2021, the maturity proceeds are tax-free under
Section 10(10D) only if the aggregate annual premium across all such ULIPs held by the
individual does not exceed ₹2,50,000 in any year during the policy term.

from these policies are instead taxed as capital gains.

Section 54: Long-term Capital Gains earned on the Sale of a Residential Property
About the Exemption:
The asset transferred should be a long-term capital asset, being a residential house
property and the capital gains should be reinvested in a residential house property only.
Conditions for Exemption:
Within a period of one year before or two years after the date of transfer of old house,
the taxpayer should acquire another residential house or should construct a residential
house within a period of three years from the date of transfer of the old house.
Can be claimed only in respect of one residential house property purchased /
constructed in India.
Once-in-a-lifetime, taxpayer can claim exemption on up to two houses if total gains do not exceed ₹2 crore.

[page 18]
Section 54F
Capital Gains Tax on Investments 18
Section 54F: Long-term Capital Gains earned on Sale of any asset other than Residential Property
About the Exemption:
The asset transferred should be a long-term capital asset, other than a residential house
property and the sale proceeds should be reinvested in one residential house property
only.
Conditions for Exemption:
Similar to exemption conditions u/s 54 but difference here is that exemption is
proportionate to sale proceeds invested.
Illustration - Sell shares worth of ₹1 crore and LTCG is ₹40 lakhs
 1) Scenario 1 – Purchased house property worth of ₹80 lakhs (80% of sale proceeds 
 reinvested).
 Exemption is only 80% of LTCG, which is ₹32 lakhs (₹8 lakhs is taxable).
 2) Scenario 2 – Purchased house property worth of ₹1 crore (100% of sale proceeds 
 reinvested).
 Exemption is 100% of LTCG, which is ₹40 lakhs.
Taxpayer should not have more than 1 house property in his name at the time of
investment into the new house property.
Maximum exemption capped at ₹10 crore on capital gains. If gains exceed this, only ₹10 crore qualifies for
exemption; balance remains taxable.

Capital Gains Account Scheme (CGAS) is a scheme for individuals to park their long-term capital
gains until they can invest it as specified in Sections 54 and 54F.

n Account Scheme

gains until they can invest it as specified in Sections 54 and 54F.
How it Works - Deposit unutilized gains in CGAS before filing ITR.
Two Types
CGAS Type A - Savings account-like, flexible withdrawals.
CGAS Type B - Fixed deposit-like, for planned investments.

Capital gains must be invested in bonds that are redeemable after five years and issued

Capital Gains Tax on Investments 21
Reporting capital gains accurately and fulfilling the necessary filing requirements is essential to
comply with tax regulations. Here are the key aspects to consider:
Individuals who have earned capital gains during the financial year are required to file their
income tax returns.
The applicable ITR form depends on the individual's income sources, residential status, and
other factors. Typically, capital gains are reported in Schedule CG of the ITR forms.
It is crucial to choose the correct ITR form and provide accurate information related to
capital gains to avoid any penalties or legal issues.
Calculation and Reporting
Capital gains should be calculated separately for each capital asset sold during the financial
year.
Short-term and long-term capital gains should be reported separately, along with relevant
details such as the cost of acquisition, sale price, and holding period.
Ensure proper documentation and maintenance of records related to the transactions,
including invoices, sale deeds, brokerage statements, and any other supporting documents.

[page 22]
Tax Payment
36.5 - Reporting & Filing Requirements
Capital Gains Tax on Investments 22
Capital gains tax liabilities should be fulfilled by paying the applicable tax amount. The tax
can be paid through the advance tax or self-assessment tax mechanisms.
In the case of short-term capital gains, the tax liability is calculated based on the individual's
applicable income tax slab rates.
For long-term capital gains, the tax rate varies depending on the type of asset and whether
indexation benefit is availed.
Due Dates and Timelines
The due date for filing the income tax return in India is given below
Individuals with tax liability exceeding ₹10,000 in a year must pay Advance Tax in four
installments during the financial year - Every 15th of June, Sep, Dec, March
However, it is advisable to keep track of any updates or changes in the due dates, as they
may vary based on individual circumstances or extensions granted by the tax authorities.
July 31st – Salaried Individuals
August 31st - Non-Audit (Business/Profession)
October 31st - Audit Cases (Business/Profession)
December 31st – Belated Returns
March 31st – Revised Returns

Non-compliance with reporting and filing requirements may lead to penalties and legal
consequences.
Late filing of the income tax return can attract penalties, and incorrect reporting of capital

with reporting and filing requirements may lead to penalties and legal
consequences.
Late filing of the income tax return can attract penalties, and incorrect reporting of capital
gains may result in tax scrutiny or reassessment by the tax department.
It is important to adhere to the timelines, accurately report capital gains, and maintain
proper documentation to avoid any penalties or unnecessary hassles.

[page 23]
Professional Guidance
Given the complexities and evolving nature of tax laws, it is advisable to seek guidance
from tax professionals, chartered accountants, or certified financial planners to ensure
accurate reporting and compliance.
Professionals can provide expert advice, help with tax planning, and assist in optimizing tax
benefits while complying with the regulations.
By adhering to the reporting and filing requirements, individuals can fulfil their tax
obligations, avoid penalties, and maintain transparency with the tax authorities. It is crucial
to stay updated with any changes in tax laws and consult professionals for accurate and up-

[slide 26]

Section - 54
Long-term capital gains earned on the Sale of a Residential Property.
About the Exemption:
The asset transferred should be a long-term capital asset, being a residential house property and the capital gains should be reinvested in a residential house property only.
Conditions for Exemption:
Within a period of one year before or two years after the date of transfer of old house, the taxpayer should acquire another residential house or should construct a residential house within a period of three years from the date of transfer of the old house.
Can be claimed only in respect of one residential house property purchased / constructed in India.
Once-in-a-lifetime, taxpayer can claim exemption on up to two houses if total gains do not exceed ₹2 crore.

[slide 27]
27
Section – 54F
Long-term capital gains are earned on the Sale of any asset other than a Residential Property.
About the Exemption:
The asset transferred should be a long-term capital asset, other than a residential house property and the sale proceeds should be reinvested in one residential house property only.
Conditions for Exemption:
Similar to exemption conditions u/s 54 but difference here is that exemption is proportionate to sale proceeds invested.
Taxpayer should not have more than 1 house property in his name at the time of investment into the new house property.

[slide 28]
28
Section – 54F
Illustration - Sell shares worth of ₹1 crore and LTCG is ₹40 lakhs
Scenario 1
Purchased house property worth of ₹80 lakhs (80% of sale proceeds reinvested).
Exemption is only 80% of LTCG, which is ₹32 lakhs (₹8 lakhs is taxable).
Scenario 2
Purchased house property worth of ₹1 crore (100% of sale proceeds reinvested).
Exemption is 100% of LTCG, which is ₹40 lakhs.
Maximum exemption capped at ₹10 crore on capital gains.
If gains exceed this, only ₹10 crore qualifies for exemption; balance remains taxable.
